title: Overview
description: Igris helps engineers run AI tasks with governed, verifiable execution.
content: Igris Request -> Execute -> Verify Request Execute Verify What To Expect From The Current Product Recommended Path Find By Goal Advanced Directions # Igris Igris helps engineers run AI tasks with governed, verifiable execution. Direct provider calls are still the right tool for simple chat or one-off prompting. Igris becomes useful when AI output starts doing work: calling tools, crossing system boundaries, touching customer data, or triggering decisions that need to be reviewed later. The simplest mental model is: 1. **Request** through one Igris API surface. 2. **Execute** with governance, routing, events, and failure handling. 3. **Verify** with signed records and verification-ready receipts. --- ## Request -> Execute -> Verify ### Request Send a request once. The surface can be a registered action run, a durable task submission, or an MCP tool call — different doors into the same system. The point is not "many products." The point is one execution system that can accept work in a stable, inspectable way. ### Execute Igris decides how the run should proceed for the deployment you have configured. That can include routing to a runtime, applying capability and policy boundaries, capturing execution events, and surfacing failure paths instead of hiding them behind a plain model response. ### Verify Igris returns more than output text. The system can also return execution metadata, signed execution records, and receipt material that can be checked after the run. That is the difference between "the model answered" and "the execution can be inspected." --- ## What To Expect From The Current Product **Governed execution.** Igris is built for runs that need boundaries, not just completions. Capability checks, policy controls, and execution-state visibility are part of the product story. **Execution visibility.** The system tracks route decisions, execution metadata, and receipt-oriented records so engineers can inspect what happened after a run. **Verification-ready records.** Signed envelopes and receipts are part of the product today, and the local unified proof demonstrates signature and hash verification on the proof-backed path. **Honest proof status.** The strongest proven path today is the local unified proof with a mock upstream. Real-provider mode is wired, but it requires sanctioned credentials and was not proven in the prior environment. title: Agent Lifecycle
description: Every agent running on the execution engine has a tracked lifecycle. State transitions are deterministic, signed, and queryable through the local runtime state API.
content: Agent Lifecycle States State Transitions Querying Agent State Get the state for one local runtime agent Lifecycle Records Canceling In-Flight Work Safe Idle (Human-in-the-Loop) Recovery # Agent Lifecycle Every agent running on the execution engine has a tracked lifecycle. State transitions are deterministic, signed, and queryable — giving you a full audit trail of every agent's history from initialization to termination. --- ## States | State | Meaning | |---|---| | `INIT` | Agent registered, not yet started | | `RUNNING` | Actively processing a request | | `IDLE` | Waiting for the next request | | `DEGRADED` | Repeated failures; execution continues with reduced confidence | | `SAFE_IDLE` | Paused pending human review or approval | | `RECOVERING` | Restarting after a violation or crash | | `TERMINATED` | Permanently stopped; no further requests accepted | --- ## State Transitions INIT → RUNNING RUNNING → IDLE (request completed normally) RUNNING → DEGRADED (error threshold exceeded) RUNNING → SAFE_IDLE (human approval required) IDLE → RUNNING (new request received) DEGRADED → RECOVERING (recovery triggered) RECOVERING → IDLE (recovery succeeded) RECOVERING → TERMINATED (recovery failed) SAFE_IDLE → RUNNING (approval granted) SAFE_IDLE → TERMINATED (approval denied) * → TERMINATED (explicit shutdown or fatal error) --- ## Querying Agent State bash # Get the state for one local runtime agent curl http://localhost:8080/v1/runtime/agent/agent-abc/state \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "state": "IDLE", "created_at": "2026-03-01T10:00:00Z", "last_transition": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "total_requests": 47, "violations": 0 } The current local runtime API exposes state for a single known agent ID. Fleet-wide runtime lists are available through the swarm and fleet coordination APIs rather than the agent lifecycle endpoint. --- ## Lifecycle Records Each state transition is recorded as a signed lifecycle event: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "from_state": "RUNNING", "to_state": "IDLE", "trigger": "request_completed", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "signature": "sha256:d4e1..." } Lifecycle records are hash-chained and included in the audit log alongside execution receipts. --- ## Canceling In-Flight Work bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/runtime/task/task-abc/cancel \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Cancellation is task-scoped in the current runtime API. A canceled task is recorded in the runtime task history and its receipt/WAL evidence remains available for reconciliation. --- #

description: Generate safe MCP and CLI setup for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and custom agents using the starter Action Pack.
content: Agent Templates Quick Path Built-in Templates Commands Verification Without Credentials Related Guides # Agent Templates Agent Templates are local configuration helpers. They do not execute actions themselves — they generate files and commands that point at the existing Igris CLI, REST Actions API, and MCP `call_action` surface. Use templates after installing the Igris CLI and exporting credential **names** locally (`IGRIS_API_URL`, `IGRIS_API_KEY`). Generated files list env var names only; never commit API key values. ## Quick Path bash export IGRIS_API_URL="https://overture.igrisinertial.com" export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_..." igris templates list igris templates install claude-code igris templates verify claude-code `install` writes to `.igris/templates/ /` by default. Use `--print` to emit files to stdout without writing, or `--dry-run` to preview paths. Optional: install the starter pack during template install when credentials are set: bash igris templates install codex --install-pack ## Built-in Templates | Name | Purpose | |---|---| | `claude-code` | Claude Code MCP config (`igris mcp serve`) | | `codex` | Terminal/CLI instructions for Codex-style agents | | `cursor` | `.cursor/mcp.json` plus CLI fallback | | `custom-agent` | REST `POST /v1/actions/:name/run` and MCP notes | All templates recommend the **starter** Action Pack (`demo.echo`, `demo.fail_once`, `demo.needs_approval`). ## Commands bash igris templates show claude-code igris templates install cursor --output ./my-agent-setup igris templates install custom-agent --print igris templates verify cursor --api-url "$IGRIS_API_URL" ## Verification Without Credentials If `IGRIS_API_KEY` is unset, `igris templates verify` prints next steps instead of failing with a stack trace. Set credentials and re-run, or follow the printed setup commands manually. ## Related Guides - [First Agent Onboarding](/docs/first-agent-onboarding) - [GET /v1/action-packs](/docs/api-reference/action-packs/get-v1-action-packs) - [POST /v1/actions/:name/run](/docs/api-reference/actions/post-v1-actions-name-run) - [MCP Server](/docs/mcp-server)

title: Agents
description: Igris supports four agent patterns: reflection, planning, tool use, and swarms. All run inside the execution envelope with full governance applied.
content: Agents Reflection Agents Planning Agents Tool-Use Agents Multi-Agent Swarms MCP Swarm Mode Agent Lifecycle Choosing the Right Agent Pattern Mode Flags Monitoring Agent State Context Engineering # Agents Igris supports four agent patterns: reflection, planning, tool use, and swarms. All run inside the execution envelope with full governance applied. --- ## Reflection Agents A reflection agent generates an initial response, evaluates its own quality, and regenerates if the quality score falls below a threshold. **Execution loop:** 1. Generate initial response 2. Score response on a 0.0–1.0 quality scale 3. If score ≥ threshold: return response 4. If score < threshold: regenerate with critique feedback 5. Repeat until threshold met or `max_steps` reached **Configuration:** json { "mode": "reflection", "reflection_threshold": 0.8, "max_reflection_steps": 3 } **When to use:** Tasks where response quality must meet a minimum bar before the result is returned — code generation, structured output, reasoning tasks. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Planning Agents A planning agent breaks down complex tasks into steps, executes each step, observes the result, and adjusts the plan before proceeding. **Execution loop:** Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect → Plan (repeat) The agent maintains a working plan that is revised after each step. Planning steps consume `max_steps` from the execution envelope. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "planning", "max_steps": 10 } **When to use:** Multi-step tasks where the approach depends on intermediate results — research, code generation with testing, multi-stage workflows. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Tool-Use Agents A tool-use agent can call external tools as part of inference: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. Tool calls are governed by the execution envelope's capability grants. Available tools (each requires an explicit capability grant): | Tool | Capability | What it does | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | GET/POST to external APIs | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands (sandboxed) | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, list files | Tool calls are recorded in the execution receipt including the call parameters, response, and latency. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "tools", "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": true } } [Tools →](/docs/tools) · [Capability Model →](/docs/capability-model) --- ## Multi-Agent Swarms A swarm executes a task using multiple specialized agents in parallel. title: API Reference
description: Customer-facing API guides and endpoint reference for Igris.
content: API Reference Start Here Action Packs Actions Platform Health Inference & Integration Runtime Distribution & Fleet Coordination Account, Trial, and Billing Vault, Policy, and Governance Execution, History, and Receipts Routing Control & Analytics Behavior Trees Durable Tasks MCP Transport Local Runtime API # API Reference This is the customer-facing API contract for Igris. Use the guide pages first, then move into the grouped endpoint reference when you are implementing or debugging a specific route. ## Start Here - [Introduction](/docs/api-reference/introduction) — How the Igris API reference is organized, when to use each access point, and how to move from guides into endpoint-level integration work. - [Authentication](/docs/api-reference/authentication) — Which credentials belong to automation, browser sessions, and runtime-local deployments, and how to choose the right one for each route. - [Errors](/docs/api-reference/errors) — How to read error responses across the API reference and what to expect from validation, authentication, throttling, and server failures. - [Rate Limits](/docs/api-reference/rate-limits) — What throttling exists today, where it applies, and how clients should behave when they receive a 429 response. ## Action Packs Built-in Action Packs install safe registered actions for first-agent onboarding. A pack is a small manifest of action definitions — it does not execute raw tasks, call external providers, or store secrets. After install, run actions through the normal Actions API or MCP `call_action` like any other registered action. - [`GET /v1/action-packs`](/docs/api-reference/action-packs/get-v1-action-packs) — Lists built-in Action Packs available for install into the authenticated tenant. - [`POST /v1/action-packs/:name/install`](/docs/api-reference/action-packs/post-v1-action-packs-name-install) — Installs a built-in Action Pack by registering its actions in your tenant. Installed actions are normal registered actions — not raw task submissions. ## Actions Registered actions are the primary execution gateway. Define what work an agent is allowed to ask Igris to run, then run those actions through Igris with policy, tenant-scoped idempotency, runtime routing, recovery, and proof. - [`GET /v1/actions`](/docs/api-reference/actions/get-v1-actions) — Lists the registered actions owned by the authenticated tenant. - [`POST /v1/actions`](/docs/api-reference/actions/post-v1-actions) — Creates a registered action definition: the contract for what an agent may ask Igris to run. - [`GET /v1/actions/:id`](/docs/api-reference/actions/get-v1-actions-id) — Gets one registered action definition by id. - [`PATCH /v1/actions/:id`](/docs/api-refere

content: POST /v1/actions When To Use Integration Guidance Common Mistakes Related Endpoints Related Guides Request Body Request Example Code Examples cURL JavaScript Go Rust Sample Response Status Codes # POST /v1/actions Creates a registered action definition. The definition declares the execution target, the HTTP method, and the policy that governs every run: preset, replay class, approval requirement, and irreversibility. Once registered, agents run the action by name — they never define execution payloads themselves. Method POST Path /v1/actions Base URL https://overture.igrisinertial.com Auth Session cookie or igris_ API key Surface Cloud API Stability stable Support core Deployment cloud ## When To Use Use this endpoint when setting up a new capability for your agents. Register the action once, then hand agents the action name and an API key. Action names are unique within your tenant. ## Integration Guidance Creation is not idempotent by key, but a retried create with the same name fails safely with `409 action_name_conflict` rather than creating a duplicate. ### Common Mistakes - Forgetting `target_url` for `hosted_api` or `webhook` actions — the action registers, but runs fail with `target_not_configured` until a target is set. - Putting secret values in `secret_refs`. The field holds secret *names* only; values are configured on the execution target. - Using an action name with uppercase letters or dashes. title: POST /v1/actions/:name/run
description: Runs a registered action by name. This is the endpoint agents call in production.
content: POST /v1/actions/:name/run When To Use Integration Guidance Common Mistakes Related Endpoints Related Guides Path Parameters Request Body Request Example Notes Code Examples cURL JavaScript Go Rust Sample Response Status Codes # POST /v1/actions/:name/run Runs a registered action by name inside the authenticated tenant. This is the endpoint agents call in production: one stable URL per action, with policy, tenant-scoped idempotency, runtime routing, recovery, and proof handled by Igris. Only registered actions can run, and tenant identity always comes from your credential, never from the request body. Method POST Path /v1/actions/:name/run Base URL https://overture.igrisinertial.com Auth Session cookie or igris_ API key Surface Cloud API Stability stable Support core Deployment cloud ## When To Use Use this endpoint as the standard way for an agent or service to execute one of your registered actions. Give the agent the action name and a tenant API key; everything else — what the action may do and where it runs — is governed by the registered definition. ## Integration Guidance Send an `idempotency_key` whenever a retry could double-run real work. Retries with the same key inside your tenant return the original run instead of starting a new one. Without a key, treat a timeout as unknown-outcome: inspect recent runs before resubmitting. ### Common Mistakes - Retrying a run without an `idempotency_key` and double-running a side effect that mattered. - Treating a `409 approval_required` response as an error. For human-gated actions it is the expected pause: the run resumes after a reviewer approves it. - Running a `local_runtime` action before a runtime is connected. The gateway refuses with `503 runtime_unavailable` instead of queueing work that cannot execute. ### Related Endpoints - [GET /v1/actions](/docs/api-reference/actions/get-v1-actions) - [POST /v1/actions](/docs/api-reference/actions/post-v1-actions) - [GET /v1/actions/:id](/docs/api-reference/actions/get-v1-actions-id) ### Related Guides - [API Authentication](/docs/api-reference/authentication) - [API Errors](/docs/api-reference/errors) - [First Agent Onboarding](/docs/first-agent-onboarding) ## Path Parameters | Field | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `name` | `string` | Yes | Name of the registered action: lowercase letters, digits, underscores, and dots (for example `demo.echo`). | ## Request Body | Field | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `input` | `object` | Yes | Input for this run, passed to the action target. title: API Authentication
description: Authentication models for cloud and local API use.
content: Authentication Tenant API Keys Session Cookies Runtime-local Auth Choosing a Credential Bearer Example Example JSON # Authentication Which credentials belong to automation, browser sessions, and runtime-local deployments, and how to choose the right one for each route. ## Tenant API Keys Customer automation should use tenant API keys with the `igris_` prefix. These keys are the default credential for server-side integrations, CI jobs, backend workers, and any script that is calling the hosted API outside the browser. Supply the key as `Authorization: Bearer ...` or `X-API-Key` if the endpoint allows it. Endpoint pages call out the expected model explicitly, so treat the endpoint page as authoritative over any generic assumption. ## Session Cookies Browser-driven console workflows use session cookies. These routes are designed for an authenticated user session rather than headless automation, so they should not be treated as generic bearer-token endpoints unless the endpoint page says an API key is also accepted. If you are building automation, prefer routes that are documented with API-key access. ## Runtime-local Auth The local runtime API follows the runtime `auth` configuration. Some deployments intentionally keep that surface inside a trusted network boundary with minimal local auth, while others front it with stricter controls. Because that access model depends on deployment, do not assume that a local runtime route behaves like the hosted API. ## Choosing a Credential Use tenant API keys for server-to-server automation. Use session cookies for browser experiences that are already inside the Igris console. Use runtime-local authentication only when the endpoint is explicitly local and you control the deployment boundary. ## Bearer Example text curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" \ https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/actions ## Example JSON json { "error": "unauthorized", "code": "INVALID_API_KEY" } API authentication bearer api key session cookie runtime auth

Method POST Path /v1/tasks/submit Base URL https://overture.igrisinertial.com Auth Session cookie or igris_ API key Surface Cloud API Stability stable Support supported Deployment cloud ## When To Use Use this endpoint when the unit of work is too long-lived, multi-step, or failure-sensitive for an ordinary synchronous inference call. It is the right contract for workflows that must survive runtime interruption and resume from durable state. ## Integration Guidance Prefer an idempotency key and treat retries as deliberate. If submission fails ambiguously, check for the existing task record before replaying the same workload. ### Common Mistakes - Submitting a workflow without an idempotency key even though the caller may retry on timeout or network failure. - Using durable tasks for simple synchronous inference that would have been clearer on the standard inference routes. - Nesting another `task_type` object inside `task_definition` instead of using the public request shape. ### Related Endpoints - [GET /v1/tasks/:id](/docs/api-reference/durable-tasks/get-v1-tasks-id) - [GET /v1/tasks](/docs/api-reference/durable-tasks/get-v1-tasks) - [GET /v1/tasks/:id/steps](/docs/api-reference/durable-tasks/get-v1-tasks-id-steps) ### Related Guides - [API Authentication](/docs/api-reference/authentication) - [API Errors](/docs/api-reference/errors) - [Context Engineering](/docs/context-engineering) ## Request Body | Field | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `task_type` | `string` | Yes | Task category. title: API Errors
description: Error handling and common response codes.
content: Errors Status Codes Validation Errors Authentication Failures Server Errors Handling Strategy Error Envelope Example JSON Common Status Codes # Errors How to read error responses across the API reference and what to expect from validation, authentication, throttling, and server failures. ## Status Codes The HTTP status code tells you what class of failure happened before you look at the JSON body. Treat 4xx responses as request, authentication, or access problems that your client should handle directly, and treat 5xx responses as server-side failures that may require retry, fallback, or operator attention. The most common patterns are 400 for invalid request shape, 401 for missing or invalid credentials, 403 for an authenticated request that still is not allowed, 404 when the addressed resource does not exist, 429 when throttling is applied, and 500-level codes when the server cannot complete a valid request. ## Validation Errors Validation failures usually mean the request shape was wrong for the route you called. Many handlers return a compact JSON envelope with `error` and sometimes a more specific `message` or `code` value that tells you what part of the request could not be accepted. ## Authentication Failures Authentication failures typically return HTTP 401. Session-based handlers often use codes such as `MISSING_SESSION` or `INVALID_SESSION`, while API-key handlers more commonly return `INVALID_API_KEY`. ## Server Errors Server-side failures commonly return a generic error such as `internal_error` or a route-specific code such as `registration_failed` or `STORAGE_FAILED`. These responses indicate that the server accepted the route contract but could not complete the operation. ## Handling Strategy Good clients do not handle every error the same way. Fix the request for 400-class validation issues, refresh or replace credentials for 401 responses, stop and inspect authorization assumptions on 403 responses, and apply controlled retry or fallback only for the routes and statuses that are documented as retry-safe. ## Error Envelope text { "error": "invalid_request", "message": "Failed to parse request body" } ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 400 | Bad Request | The route was reached, but the request body, query, or path data did not match the endpoint contract. | | 401 | Unauth API errors error codes invalid request unauthorized internal error

Method GET Path /v1/receipts/export Base URL https://overture.igrisinertial.com Auth Session cookie or igris_ API key Surface Cloud API Stability stable Support supported Deployment cloud ## When To Use Use this endpoint when receipt data needs to leave the product boundary for BI, compliance, archive, or offline analysis. title: API Introduction
description: Overview of the customer API contract.
content: Introduction Two Product Surfaces How Endpoint Pages Work First-Agent Onboarding Path SDK Guidance Support Labels and Deployment Modes Base URLs Example JSON # Introduction How the Igris API reference is organized, when to use each access point, and how to move from guides into endpoint-level integration work. ## Two Product Surfaces Igris is documented here as one product with two access points. Use the hosted API at `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` for registered actions, runs, MCP, account, fleet, receipt, and policy capabilities. Use the local runtime API at `http://localhost:8080` by default when the request belongs on the machine where Igris is running. This split is about where the request executes, not about two different products. The API reference groups endpoints by capability so you can navigate by task first and only think about the base URL when you are ready to make the call. ## How Endpoint Pages Work Every endpoint has its own page. That page tells you what the route is for, which authentication model it expects, the path and query parameters it accepts, the request body fields that matter, and the status codes you should plan for in a real client. Use the overview page to browse by capability, then switch to endpoint pages when you are implementing or debugging a specific call. ## First-Agent Onboarding Path If you are wiring a new agent, start with the **Action Packs** section: list built-in packs, install the `starter` pack, then run `demo.echo` through **Actions** (`POST /v1/actions/:name/run`) or MCP `call_action`. Action Packs register safe actions — they do not execute raw tasks or ship live external connectors. See [First Agent Onboarding](/docs/first-agent-onboarding) for the full CLI and MCP walkthrough. ## SDK Guidance JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, and Python are the first-class SDK languages today. When an endpoint is covered by a native SDK, prefer that SDK for application code because it gives you a cleaner call surface and reduces request-shape drift over time. Some management routes are still best treated as direct HTTP integrations. In those cases, the endpoint page is the primary contract: use the request and response examples, confirm the authentication model, and wire your own client behavior around the listed status codes. ## Support Labels and Deployment Modes Each endpoint page carries both a support label and a deployment mode. **Core** routes are the primary customer contract. **Supported** routes are part of the shipped product surface but may not be the first end API introduction base URL surfaces overview contract

title: API Rate Limits
description: Rate limit behavior and retry expectations.
content: Rate Limits Global Control-plane Limit Runtime Download Limit Client Behavior 429 Example Example JSON Common Status Codes # Rate Limits What throttling exists today, where it applies, and how clients should behave when they receive a 429 response. ## Global Control-plane Limit The hosted API currently applies a default limiter of 100 requests per minute. Endpoint pages call out the exceptions that matter more than the global default. Response headers are only guaranteed on the 429 path right now. Clients should not assume that every successful response carries full rate-limit metadata. ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime download endpoints use a tighter subscription-aware throttle. Treat binary download as a provisioning or rollout action, not as a hot-path request that your application makes repeatedly during normal traffic. ## Client Behavior Build clients so that a 429 is expected and handled, not treated as an exceptional edge case. Honor `Retry-After` when it is present, apply backoff with jitter for repeated retries, and avoid running parallel request bursts that all wake up at the same second. ## 429 Example text Retry-After: 60 X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 429 | Too Many Requests | Retry after the advertised cooldown window. | API rate limits retry-after 429 throttle

content: DELETE /api/v1/runtime/deregister When To Use Integration Guidance Common Mistakes Related Endpoints Related Guides Request Body Request Example Code Examples cURL JavaScript Go Rust Sample Response Status Codes # DELETE /api/v1/runtime/deregister Marks a runtime as deregistered and unhealthy for the current tenant. The runtime remains in historical records but should no longer be treated as an active fleet member. title: Human-in-the-Loop Approvals
description: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval pauses an execution run before it completes a high-stakes action. A reviewer must explicitly approve or reject the run before execution continues.
content: Human-in-the-Loop Approvals How Executions Get Paused for Review Finding Runs Waiting for Approval Reviewing in the Console Approving a Run → {"status": "RUNNING", "approved": true} Rejecting a Run → {"status": "REJECTED", "reason": "action_out_of_scope"} What Gets Recorded in the Receipt Replaying a Rejected Run → {"status": "replayed", "new_execution_id": "exec-01HABC"} Monitoring the Approval Queue Best Practices # Human-in-the-Loop Approvals Human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval pauses an execution run before it completes a high-stakes action. A reviewer must explicitly approve or reject the run before execution continues. The full approval event — who made the decision, when, and why — is recorded in the signed execution receipt and cannot be altered after the fact. --- ## How Executions Get Paused for Review The execution engine evaluates review triggers as each run progresses. Triggers are configured in your policy and can match on tool call targets, output classifications, capability combinations, or custom conditions. When a trigger fires, the run transitions from RUNNING to **PAUSED** with `pause_reason: human_review_required`. The run holds open in that state indefinitely — it does not time out and does not progress — until a human makes a deliberate approve or reject decision. The execution envelope remains intact while the run is paused. Resources are reserved and the agent's context is preserved. Once a decision is made, the run either continues (approve) or terminates (reject) from exactly the point where it was paused. --- ## Finding Runs Waiting for Approval Query paused runs via the API: bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/execution/runs?status=PAUSED" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "execution_id": "exec-01HXYZ", "agent_id": "agent-abc", "status": "PAUSED", "pause_reason": "human_review_required", "paused_at": "2026-03-31T10:14:22Z", "prompt_preview": "About to POST to https://payments.example.com/disburse with amount: 4500", "runtime_id": "runtime-01" } ] The `prompt_preview` field is a brief description of what the execution was about to do at the point it was paused. It is generated by the execution engine and is not the raw model input — it is a structured summary of the pending action, designed to give a reviewer enough context to make an informed decision. --- ## Reviewing in the Console The **Execution Runs** page in the console shows all paused runs in a dedicated review queue at the top of the list. Each row shows a **Review** badge and the time the run has been waiting. Click a paused run to open its detail panel. You will see: - **Prompt preview** — the pending action description - **Agent ID** — which agent initiated this run - **Pause reason** — always `human_review_required` for HITL items - **Paused

title: Architecture
description: Igris is one execution system for AI tasks. This page maps the Request -> Execute -> Verify model onto the hosted and runtime components that implement it.
content:
Architecture System Overview Coordination Layer (Cloud Gateway) Core Capabilities Data Layer API Surface Igris Runtime (Edge Engine) Core Capabilities Trust Chain Deployment Topologies # Architecture Igris is one execution system for AI tasks. The best way to read the architecture is not "which product do I buy?" but "how does a request move through Request -> Execute -> Verify?" At a high level: - **Request** enters through an Igris API surface. - **Execute** happens on the configured hosted or runtime path, with policy, capability, and routing decisions applied along the way. - **Verify** happens through execution metadata, signed records, and receipt-oriented audit material after the run. The hosted control plane and the runtime are implementation components inside that unified model. They matter for deployment and operations, but they should not be your first mental model. --- ## System Overview Start from the execution flow, then map it to components. A request enters Igris, execution happens on the configured path, and verification data comes back with the result. Hosted and runtime surfaces are deployment choices, not separate product identities. | Layer | Responsibility | |---|---| | **Application** | Sends requests through an Igris API surface | | **Execution Control** | Applies routing, policy, runtime selection, and failure-path handling | | **Hosted Providers** | Execute hosted model work when the configured path stays in cloud infrastructure | | **Runtime** | Executes governed local or hybrid work, returns execution artifacts, and emits signed receipt material | Registration, heartbeat, receipt sync, and task handoff connect the hosted and runtime layers when you run Igris in hybrid mode. mermaid graph TD App["Your Application or Agent
(SDK or HTTP client)"] App -->|"POST /v1/actions/:name/run"| Coordination subgraph Coordination["Coordination Layer (Cloud Gateway)"] Router["Adaptive Router"] CB["Circuit Breaker"] PS["Provider Selection"] CA["Routing Advisor"] SLO["SLO Enforcer"] Vault["Key Vault
(Encrypted Storage)"] Router --> PS CB --> PS CA -.->|"recommendations"| Router SLO -.->|"enforcement"| Router end PS -->|"cloud providers"| OpenAI["OpenAI / Anthropic / Google"] PS -->|"hybrid fallback"| Runtime subgraph Runtime["Igris Runtime (Edge)"] Server["HTTP Server
(OpenAI-compatible API)"] LLM["Local LLM
(GGUF models)"] BT["Behavior Tree Engine"] Tools["Tool Sandbox
(HTTP, Shell, FS)"] Receipts["Signed Receipts
(cryptographic chain)"] MCP["MCP Server/Client"] Server --> LLM Server --> BT Server --> Tools Server --> Rece

title: Deploying Igris on Edge Devices
description: Step-by-step guide for deploying the Igris runtime on Raspberry Pi, Jetson, and other edge hardware.
content: Deploying Igris on Edge Devices Supported Edge Platforms Install The Runtime 1. Download the archive 2. Extract and install 3. Download a model 4. Configure the runtime 5. Start the runtime Run As A Service Health And Monitoring # Deploying Igris on Edge Devices Running `igris-runtime` on edge hardware gives you local inference, local policy enforcement, and a clean path to hybrid cloud coordination. --- ## Supported Edge Platforms | Platform | Architecture | Minimum RAM | Recommended starting model | |---|---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4/5 | ARM64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano | ARM64 | 8 GB | Mistral 7B (Q4) | | Generic x86_64 host | x86_64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | GPU-backed x86_64 host | x86_64 | 16 GB | 7B to 8B GGUF | --- ## Install The Runtime ### 1. Download the archive bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-arm64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the checksum output before extracting. ### 2. Extract and install bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ### 3. Download a model bash mkdir -p /opt/igris/models wget -O /opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf \ "https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-gguf/resolve/main/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf" ### 4. Configure the runtime Create `/etc/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf", n_gpu_layers: 0, threads: 4, context_size: 4096 } } Platform tuning: - **Raspberry Pi**: keep `n_gpu_layers` at `0`; tune `threads` to the available CPU cores - **Jetson**: raise `n_gpu_layers` for GPU offload and keep `threads` conservative - **GPU-backed x86_64**: increase `n_gpu_layers` based on VRAM capacity ### 5. Start the runtime bash igris-runtime serve If you want the device to appear in Fleet, also set `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` before startup. --- ## Run As A Service Example `systemd` unit: ini [Unit] Description=Igris Runtime After=network.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=/home/igris/.local/bin/igris-runtime serve Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 User=igris Group=igris [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target --- ## Health And Monitoring bash curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health curl http://localhost:8080/

title: Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates
description: A practical guide to configuring capability grants, monitoring violations, and iterating on your agent policies.
content: Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates The Capability Model Available Capabilities Start Restrictive, Expand as Needed Step 1: Deploy with No Capabilities Step 2: Review Violations Step 3: Grant Legitimate Capabilities Step 4: Iterate Capability Patterns by Agent Type Read-Only Analyst API Integration Agent Automation Agent DevOps Agent Monitoring and Alerting Console Monitoring API Monitoring Reviewing Violations Common Pitfalls Over-Granting Capabilities Ignoring Violations Not Using Shadow Mode # Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates When agents can make HTTP requests, execute shell commands, or access the filesystem, the risk surface grows significantly. Igris's capability gates ensure that agents can only perform operations you explicitly authorize. --- ## The Capability Model Every execution in Igris runs with a **capability grant** — a declarative list of what the agent is permitted to do. The engine enforces these grants before any operation executes. ### Available Capabilities | Capability | Controls | |---|---| | `allow_http` | Outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | Specific domains the agent can call | | `allow_shell` | Shell command execution | | `allowed_shell_commands` | Specific commands the agent can run | | `allow_filesystem` | File read/write operations | | `allowed_filesystem_paths` | Specific paths the agent can access | | `max_file_write_bytes` | Maximum bytes the agent can write | --- ## Start Restrictive, Expand as Needed The safest approach is to start with no capabilities granted and add them incrementally: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 1: Deploy with No Capabilities Deploy your agent with all capabilities disabled. Run it against real traffic in **shadow mode** to observe what it would do without actually executing. ### Step 2: Review Violations Check the **Proof → Violations** page in the console. Each violation shows: - Which capability was attempted - Which agent attempted it - When it happened ### Step 3: Grant Legitimate Capabilities For violations that represent legitimate agent behavior, grant the specific capability: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allowed_http_domains": ["api.example.com", "cdn.example.com"], "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 4: Iterate Repeat steps 2–3 until your agent operates without violations. This process typically takes 1–3 iterations for well-designed agents. --- ## Capability Patterns by Agent Type ### Read-Only Analyst An agent that analyzes data and produces reports: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } No tools needed. The agent works purely with its training knowledge and the provided context. ### API Integration Agent An agent that calls external APIs: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": tr

title: Adaptive Path Selection in Igris
description: How Igris can choose between configured execution paths and providers as an advanced part of the Execute stage.
content: Adaptive Path Selection in Igris Where It Fits What The System Actually Tracks Advanced Strategies What To Inspect After A Run Related Pages # Adaptive Path Selection in Igris Path selection is an advanced part of the **Execute** stage in Igris. The main product value is not the algorithm itself. The value is that Igris can choose a configured execution path, record what happened, and return metadata and signed records you can inspect later. --- ## Where It Fits Use adaptive path selection when: - you have more than one provider or execution path configured - you want execution to react to health, latency, or policy constraints - you need those choices recorded as part of the run If you only call one provider directly, you may not need any of this. --- ## What The System Actually Tracks Igris can track recent execution outcomes such as: - provider or path used - success or failure - latency - cost metadata where available Those signals can inform later path selection. The important operational outcome is that the decision becomes part of the execution record rather than an invisible client-side guess. --- ## Advanced Strategies Some deployments use adaptive strategies such as Thompson-sampling-style selection or other cost- or latency-oriented policies. Treat those as advanced execution mechanisms: - they belong under the Execute stage - they are not the first reason to adopt Igris - performance outcomes depend on workload, configuration, and provider behavior Avoid assuming a benchmark or latency gain unless you have measured it in your own environment. --- ## What To Inspect After A Run When advanced path selection is enabled, operators should inspect: - which path or provider was chosen - whether a fallback path was taken - what the final execution status was - which receipt or signed record corresponds to the run That is where Igris differs from a thin routing proxy: execution decisions remain reviewable. --- ## Related Pages - [Request -> Execute -> Verify →](/docs/request-execute-verify) - [Execution Flow →](/docs/execution-flow) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status) - [All Articles →](/docs/articles)

title: Audit
description: How Igris exposes signed records, receipt queries, export workflows, and verification-related audit surfaces.
content: Audit Primary Audit Artifact Lineage Query And Export Verification Semantics Retention Related Pages # Audit Audit in Igris starts from signed records and verification-ready receipts. This page explains what operators can inspect after a run, how receipt data is queried and exported, and where verification semantics are stronger or weaker today. --- ## Primary Audit Artifact The primary audit artifact is the execution receipt. A receipt can include: - request and run identity - execution metadata - status and timing - capability or policy outcomes - tool activity where applicable - signed or hash-linked record material Use [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) for the receipt-oriented explanation and [Verification](/docs/verification) for the verification model. --- ## Lineage Igris keeps lineage between request submission, execution activity, and post-run inspection surfaces. That lets operators answer questions such as: - which request created this run - which execution path was taken - what events were emitted - which receipt corresponds to the final outcome --- ## Query And Export Hosted audit surfaces can expose receipt listings, receipt retrieval, export workflows, and violation review. Use them to retain evidence outside the runtime when your retention or audit requirements demand it. Typical workflows are: 1. list recent receipts 2. retrieve a specific run record 3. export receipts for external audit or retention 4. inspect recorded violations or review events --- ## Verification Semantics Two verification paths matter here: - the local proof-backed path, where signed record and receipt verification are demonstrated - the hosted proof route, which confirms stored receipt values and proof status for a run Use the hosted proof route for hosted receipt review workflows, and use the local proof-backed path when you need the stronger demonstrated cryptographic verification story. --- ## Retention Receipt and audit retention depends on the environment and plan you operate with. For stronger retention requirements: - export hosted records before retention windows expire - keep your own storage for local-only deployments - treat receipts and tracing as complementary, not interchangeable --- ## Related Pages - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Verification →](/docs/verification) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status) - [Observability & Tracing →](/docs/observability-tracing)

description: Igris currently exposes two behavior-tree schemas. Treat them as different layers of the product:
content: Behavior Trees 1. Cloud Definition Schema 2. Runtime Execution Schema Using the JavaScript SDK Using the Go SDK Practical Rule Durable Execution # Behavior Trees Igris currently exposes **two** behavior-tree schemas. Treat them as different layers of the product: - The **definition schema** used by the cloud control plane and console editor - The **runtime execution schema** used by the runtime API and native SDKs If you mix them up, validation will fail. --- ## 1. Cloud Definition Schema The coordination layer stores graph-style definitions using `nodes` and `edges`. json { "name": "shutdown-guard", "description": "Temperature-triggered shutdown sequence", "nodes": [ , , ], "edges": [ , ] } This is the schema used by: - `GET /v1/bt/templates` - `GET /v1/bt/definitions` - `GET /v1/bt/definitions/:id` - `POST /v1/bt/definitions` - `DELETE /v1/bt/definitions/:id` --- ## 2. Runtime Execution Schema The runtime and native SDKs use a nested tree representation with lowercase node types. json { "type": "sequence", "name": "shutdown-guard", "children": [ { "type": "condition", "name": "check_temp", "key": "sensor.temperature", "expected": "80" }, { "type": "action", "name": "shutdown", "tool": "http_post", "args": { "url": "http://localhost:9000/shutdown" } } ] } This is the schema accepted by the local runtime endpoints: - `POST /v1/btree/validate` - `POST /v1/btree/run` - `POST /v1/btree/deploy` --- ## Using the JavaScript SDK typescript import { Runtime, BehaviorTree, SequenceNode, ConditionNode, ActionNode, } from '@igris-inertial/sdk'; const runtime = new Runtime( ); const tree = BehaviorTree.fromJson( new SequenceNode('shutdown-guard', [ new ConditionNode('check_temp', 'sensor.temperature', '80'), new ActionNode('shutdown', 'http_post', ), ]).toJSON(), runtime, ); const result = await tree.validate(); console.log(result.valid); --- ## Using the Go SDK go package main import ( "context" "log" igris "github.com/igris-inertial/go-sdk" ) func main() { runtime := igris.NewRuntime("http://localhost:8080") treeDef := igris.NewSequenceNode("shutdown-guard", igris.NewConditionNode("check_temp", "sensor.temperature", "80"), igris.NewActionNode("shutdown", "http_post", map[string]interface{}{ "url": "http://localhost:9000/shutdown", }), ) tree := igris.NewBehaviorTree(treeDef, runtime) if _, err := tree.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } --- ## Practical Rule Use `nodes` / `edges` only when you are talking to the cloud definition API. Use lowercase nested nodes when you are talking t

title: Capabilities & Limits
description: The execution engine enforces a capability model: every execution runs with an explicit set of permissions. If an agent tries to do something outside those permissions, the operati
content: Capabilities & Limits Capability Fields Configuration Enforcement Points Violation Records Violation Types # Capabilities & Limits The execution engine enforces a capability model: every execution runs with an explicit set of permissions. If an agent tries to do something outside those permissions, the operation is blocked before it executes and the violation is recorded in the signed receipt. --- ## Capability Fields | Capability | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `allow_http` | bool | Allow outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | string[] | Allowlist of domains for HTTP calls | | `allow_shell` | bool | Allow shell command execution | | `allow_filesystem` | bool | Allow filesystem read/write | | `max_file_write_bytes` | int | Maximum bytes the execution may write | --- ## Configuration Set capability limits in your `config.json5`: json5 { capabilities: { allow_http: true, allowed_http_domains: ["api.openweathermap.org", "api.github.com"], allow_shell: false, allow_filesystem: true, max_file_write_bytes: 1048576 // 1 MB } } Capabilities can also be set per-request via the `X-Igris-Capabilities` header for tenants with override permission. --- ## Enforcement Points **HTTP tool calls** — before each outbound request, the engine checks `allow_http` and that the target domain is in `allowed_http_domains`. Blocked calls produce a `HttpDomainNotAllowed` violation. **Shell commands** — if `allow_shell` is false and an agent attempts a shell invocation, the call is rejected with a `ShellNotAllowed` violation before the command is spawned. **Filesystem operations** — write operations are counted against `max_file_write_bytes`. Reads beyond the allowed path prefix produce a `FilesystemNotAllowed` violation. --- ## Violation Records Every blocked operation is recorded as a violation in the execution receipt: json { "capability_violations": [ { "kind": "HttpDomainNotAllowed", "detail": "Domain 'evil.com' not in allowed_http_domains", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:00:01Z" } ] } Violation records are included in the signed receipt and cannot be removed or suppressed. Compliance auditors can verify that policy enforcement was applied to every execution. --- ## Violation Types | Kind | Trigger | |---|---| | `HttpNotAllowed` | HTTP tool called but `allow_http` is false | | `HttpDomainNotAllowed` | Domain not in `allowed_http_domains` | | `ShellNotAllowed` | Shell command attempted but `allow_shell` is false | | `FilesystemNotAllowed` | Path outside allowed prefix |

title: Circuit Breaker
description: The circuit breaker is an advanced failure-aware execution mechanism that reduces traffic to unhealthy upstream paths.
content: Circuit Breaker Core States Why It Matters What It Does Not Mean How To Operate It Monitoring Related Pages # Circuit Breaker The circuit breaker is an advanced failure-aware execution mechanism. Its purpose is to reduce traffic to an upstream path that is repeatedly failing, then probe cautiously to see whether that path has recovered. This helps make failure paths more visible and controlled during execution. --- ## Core States The common state model is: - **closed** when the path is healthy enough for ordinary traffic - **open** when the path should stop receiving ordinary traffic - **half-open** when the system is probing recovery carefully This is a classic control mechanism, but in Igris it matters because it shapes which execution paths remain eligible during failure conditions. ## Why It Matters Without a breaker, the system may keep sending work into a failing path longer than it should. With a breaker, operators get: - clearer failure handling - reduced repeated attempts against a path that is already misbehaving - a more deliberate recovery probe before normal traffic resumes ## What It Does Not Mean The breaker is not a blanket guarantee that every execution survives every upstream issue. It is one mechanism in the larger Execute-stage control stack. Other layers still matter: - policy - health - trust - explicit deployment choices ## How To Operate It Use breaker settings to match your tolerance for: - repeated upstream failures - recovery probe frequency - flapping behavior If a path is bouncing rapidly between states, that is an operational signal worth inspecting rather than something to hide behind automation language. ## Monitoring Use console and API health views to inspect breaker state and recent failure behavior. Treat those views as execution diagnostics, not as proof that all survival scenarios are fully covered. ## Related Pages - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Provider Trust →](/docs/provider-trust) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) - [SLO Enforcer →](/docs/slo-enforcer)

title: Cloud Coordination
description: Hosted coordination is the part of Igris that manages provider-backed execution, runtime lifecycle surfaces, and customer-facing receipt workflows.
content: Cloud Coordination What Hosted Coordination Does Hosted Request Entry Provider Configuration Runtime Lifecycle Surfaces Receipt And Audit Surfaces Routing Details Belong Lower In The Stack Related Guides # Cloud Coordination Cloud coordination is the hosted part of the Igris execution system. Its job is to coordinate provider-backed execution, expose customer-facing management surfaces, and connect runtimes into the broader execution model when hybrid workflows are enabled. That is useful when you want: - a stable hosted entry path for applications - provider-backed execution without custom client-side routing logic - runtime lifecycle and fleet-oriented operator surfaces - customer-facing receipt and audit workflows --- ## What Hosted Coordination Does Hosted coordination can cover: - application-facing request entry - provider-backed execution setup - runtime registration and lifecycle surfaces - receipt and proof-oriented query surfaces - account, policy, and key-management workflows This is part of one execution system. It should not be read as a separate product introduction. ## Hosted Request Entry The standard hosted entry point is the actions gateway — agents run registered actions by name: text POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/actions/:name/run That keeps the application contract simple while letting Igris own policy, routing, idempotency, and evidence behind it. See [First Hosted Integration →](/docs/first-cloud-integration). ## Provider Configuration Hosted execution depends on provider credentials stored through the vault API. For customer traffic today, use `openai` or `anthropic`. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' Provider-backed execution is configurable and supported. Proof claims about specific real-provider flows should still follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status). ## Runtime Lifecycle Surfaces When hybrid workflows matter, runtimes coordinate with the hosted layer through the runtime lifecycle routes. Use the endpoint pages for the exact request contracts: - [POST /api/v1/runtime/register](/docs/api-reference/runtime-distribution-fleet-coordination/post-api-v1-runtime-register) - [POST /api/v1/runtime/heartbeat](/docs/api-reference/runtime-distribution-fleet-coordination/post-api-v1-runtime-heartbeat) - [DELETE /api/v1/runtime/deregister](/docs/api-reference/runtime-distribution-fleet-coordination/delete-api-v1-runtime-dere

title: Routing Advisor (Technical Preview)
description: An advanced operator surface for reviewing path-selection suggestions and controlled configuration changes.
content: Routing Advisor (Technical Preview) What It Does Recommended Operating Model What This Page Does Not Claim Related Pages # Routing Advisor (Technical Preview) The Routing Advisor is an advanced operator surface for reviewing suggested path-selection changes. It belongs under the **Execute** stage of Igris, not the top-level product story. The primary value is still governed execution with visible decisions, signed records, and verification-ready receipts. See [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before treating this page as a production commitment. --- ## What It Does In configurations that expose advisor functionality, the system can review recent execution outcomes and surface suggestions such as: - shifting between configured execution paths - adjusting provider preferences - changing how aggressively fallbacks are used Those suggestions should be treated as operator proposals, not automatic truth. --- ## Recommended Operating Model Use advisor-style workflows conservatively: 1. review the proposal 2. compare it with recent execution events and receipts 3. apply changes deliberately 4. watch the next runs before promoting the change further Automatic application should only be used when you understand the underlying risk and have rollback procedures in place. --- ## What This Page Does Not Claim This page does not claim: - guaranteed improvements - automatic safe optimization for every workload - proof-backed production auto-tuning across all deployments Treat any advisor-driven workflow as advanced and configuration-dependent. --- ## Related Pages - [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status)

title: Console User Guide
description: The console is the operator view for execution events, run history, signed records, environment visibility, and account management.
content: Console User Guide Dashboard Execution Runs Proof, Receipts, And Violations Execution Environments Policy And Governance Views Billing And Account Areas How To Read The Console Related Pages # Console User Guide The console is the operator view for Igris. Its main job is to help teams inspect and operate: - execution events and run history - signed records and receipt-oriented workflows - execution environments - account, policy, and billing surfaces This page focuses on the practical operator reading of the console rather than trying to document every advanced feature as if it were equally central. --- ## Dashboard The dashboard is the summary view. Use it to get a quick answer to questions like: - are execution runs active - are violations or alert-worthy events increasing - are registered environments still visible - are we approaching an environment-capacity limit Treat it as an operator snapshot, not as the source of truth for deep execution analysis. ## Execution Runs The most important console surface for many teams is the run view. Use it to inspect: - current run status - pause, cancellation, or review state - run metadata - links into receipt and follow-up workflows This is the console surface that maps most directly to the Verify stage of the product model. ## Proof, Receipts, And Violations The proof-oriented areas of the console help operators inspect: - signed or receipt-oriented records - policy-violation follow-up - what should be verified before evidence leaves the product boundary Use these views together with: - [Verification](/docs/verification) - [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Receipts and Audit Workflow](/docs/receipts-audit-workflow) ## Execution Environments The console also shows registered execution environments and their visibility state. That is useful for: - checking whether a runtime environment is registered - confirming heartbeat visibility - staging rollout work carefully The console should not be read as proof that all environment-management automation is broadly ready across every workflow. Use [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) when rollout or update claims matter. ## Policy And Governance Views Console policy and governance views are operator tools for: - checking whether boundaries are behaving as expected - investigating violations - reviewing the effect of permission and policy changes They are useful because policy only matters if the run and its results can still be inspected afterward. ## Billing And Account Areas The console also includes account and billing surfaces. title: Context Engineering
description: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what the model should see, what the runtime should remember, and what the product should preserve across steps, failures, and depl
content: Context Engineering Start With The Smallest Useful Context The Context Layers In Igris 1. Request-local context 2. Retrieval and memory 3. MCP and shared context 4. Durable task state 5. Receipts and audit context Choosing The Right Layer Implementation Checklist Common Patterns Action runs with light context Agent workflows with reusable state Hybrid deployments with shared device state Long-running workflows A Practical Product Pattern Common Mistakes What Good Context Engineering Looks Like Code And Workflow Quality Signals Related Guides # Context Engineering Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what the model should see, what the runtime should remember, and what the product should preserve across steps, failures, and deployments. In Igris, that choice matters because context can live in several different places: - the request itself - memory systems - MCP and shared context - durable-task checkpoints - receipts and audit records If you put the wrong information in the wrong layer, the system still works, but it becomes harder to reason about, more expensive to operate, and more fragile across retries, restarts, and handoffs. --- ## Start With The Smallest Useful Context The default rule is simple: give the model only the context required to succeed at the current step. That means: - put request-specific instructions and inputs in the request - put reusable knowledge in retrieval or memory - put shared operational state in an explicit shared context layer - put recovery-critical workflow state in durable tasks What you want to avoid is using the prompt as a dumping ground for everything the product knows. ## The Context Layers In Igris ### 1. Request-local context Request-local context belongs in the request payload itself: messages, task inputs, or tool-call inputs. This is the right place for information that matters only to the current call. Use this for: - the current user instruction - short-lived execution constraints - immediate tool-call inputs - one-off routing intent Do not use request-local context as a substitute for shared memory or durable state. ### 2. Retrieval and memory Use memory systems when context should survive beyond one request but does not need to become part of the durable workflow protocol. This includes: - semantic retrieval from vector memory - short-lived working state in KV-style memory - shared blackboard-style state when multiple agents need the same view Use this when the question is: "what should the next step be able to recall?" Use durable tasks instead when the question is: "what must survive an interruption and resume safely?" ### 3. MCP and shared context Use MCP when context should be shared across tools, sessions, or runtime instances in a structured way. MCP is the right layer for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented context - cross-instance context in swarm or multi-device operation Use MCP when context is part of the operating en

title: Data Privacy
description: Igris is designed with privacy as a core principle. This guide explains how your data is handled, stored, and protected across the platform.
content: Data Privacy Data We Collect Account Data Execution Data Fleet Data Provider Keys How We Handle Your Data Data Storage Data Retention Data Isolation Your Rights Data Access Data Deletion Data Portability Privacy by Deployment Mode Cloud API Mode Edge / Offline Mode Hybrid Mode Third-Party Data Sharing Cloud Providers Billing Analytics Compliance GDPR Data Processing Agreement Security Measures Contact # Data Privacy Igris is designed with privacy as a core principle. This guide explains how your data is handled, stored, and protected across the platform. --- ## Data We Collect ### Account Data - Email address and account information - Subscription tier and billing history - API key metadata (prefix only — full keys are never stored after creation) ### Execution Data - Request inputs (prompts, messages) - Model outputs and responses - Resource usage metrics (tokens, latency, cost) - Capability violations and enforcement actions - Signed execution receipts ### Fleet Data - Runtime instance identifiers and registration details - Health metrics and telemetry - Configuration state - Topic mappings (for ROS2 integrations) ### Provider Keys - Cloud provider API keys (encrypted at rest) - Key validation status and rotation history --- ## How We Handle Your Data ### Data Storage - **Cloud API users**: Execution data is stored in our managed infrastructure with encryption at rest - **Edge/Offline users**: All data stays on your device. Nothing is transmitted to Igris servers unless you explicitly export it ### Data Retention Execution records are retained according to your tier: | Tier | Retention Period | |---|---| | Seed | 7 days | | Horizon | 60 days | | Infinite | Custom retention policy | After the retention period expires, execution data is automatically purged. ### Data Isolation All data is strictly scoped by tenant. Your data is never accessible to other tenants, and Igris staff cannot view your execution content without explicit authorization. --- ## Your Rights ### Data Access You can access all data associated with your account at any time: - Export execution receipts via the API - Download your fleet configuration - View your complete audit log bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?range=30d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" ### Data Deletion You can request deletion of your account and all associated data: 1. Navigate to **Settings → Account** 2. Click **Delete Account** 3. Confirm the deletion Account deletion is permanent and irreversible. All execution records, fleet data, and configuration will be removed within 30 days. ### Data Portability You can export all your data in a structured format for migration to another system. Contact [support@igrisinertial.com](mailto:support@igrisinertial.com) for a full data ex

title: Deploy Local Runtime
description: Use this workflow when execution should happen closer to the machine, device, or environment where the work actually runs.
content: Deploy Local Runtime 1. Download The Runtime Archive 2. Install The Binary 3. Configure Auth And Local Execution Behavior 4. Start And Verify The Runtime 5. Send A Local Request Two Ways Work Reaches the Runtime Register the Runtime for Fleet and Dispatch Where the Binary Comes From What To Say Carefully Common Mistakes Related Guides # Deploy Local Runtime Use this workflow when Igris should execute closer to where the work happens. Local runtime is not a separate product identity. It is an execution surface for workloads that benefit from locality, device-level boundaries, or reduced dependence on a hosted path. Choose this path when you need: - execution near the machine or device doing the work - local policy enforcement or bounded task handling - offline or low-connectivity operation - runtime-local behavior tree or tool execution If those properties are not central to the workload, start with the hosted integration first. --- ## 1. Download The Runtime Archive Use the runtime distribution endpoints for your platform and treat download as provisioning, not application traffic. bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-amd64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the archive checksum before installation. ## 2. Install The Binary bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ## 3. Configure Auth And Local Execution Behavior Create `~/.config/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0 } } This configuration expresses how the runtime should execute work locally. Treat local GGUF fallback carefully in public claims: the code path exists, but reproducible proof should be checked against [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before you present it as a guaranteed behavior. ## 4. Start And Verify The Runtime bash igris-runtime serve curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health Once the runtime is healthy, use the runtime base URL for local requests: text http://localhost:8080/v1 ## 5. Send A Local Request typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'http://localhost:8080/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'phi3', messages: [ ], }); This is still the same execution model: - **Request** through an Igris API surf

title: Deployment
description: Choose the Igris deployment mode based on where execution should run: hosted, local, or hybrid.
content: Deployment Hosted Deployment Local Deployment Hybrid Deployment Local Models And Fallback Language Verifying A Deployment Common Deployment Issues Related Guides # Deployment Choose your deployment mode based on where execution should run. Igris is one execution system with multiple deployment modes: - **hosted** when provider-backed execution through the managed surface is enough - **local** when work should run closer to your machine or device - **hybrid** when hosted coordination and runtime participation both matter The deployment choice changes where execution happens. It does not create separate products. --- ## Hosted Deployment Use hosted deployment when you want the fastest provider-backed path with the least operational overhead. python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1", api_key="your-api-key" ) Hosted deployment is a good fit when you want: - managed API entry - provider-backed execution - simpler onboarding - customer-facing receipt and audit surfaces without local runtime operations Proof claims for specific real-provider paths should still follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status). ## Local Deployment Use local deployment when execution should happen closer to the environment doing the work. Typical reasons: - device or infrastructure locality - local tool or workflow integration - low-connectivity or offline-sensitive operation - runtime-side governance near the workload Start the runtime on your own infrastructure and point the client at the runtime base URL when the request belongs there. ## Hybrid Deployment Use hybrid deployment when you want one application-facing contract while allowing runtime participation underneath. This mode is useful when you need: - a hosted entry path for applications - runtime-backed execution in selected environments - operator visibility into registered execution environments Keep the proof language careful: - hybrid architecture is supported - not every failover or recovery behavior should be described as proven without the matching artifact See [Hybrid Deployment Workflow](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow) for the staged operator view. ## Local Models And Fallback Language Local model configuration is part of the deployment story, but language here should stay disciplined: - local execution is real - local fallback paths exist in the product model - failure-to-local-model proof should follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before being described as proven behavior ## Verifying A Deployment After you deploy,

title: Durable Task Execution
description: Use durable tasks for long-running AI work that needs state, boundaries, and records that survive beyond a single synchronous request.
content: Durable Task Execution What Durable Tasks Add How To Think About The Lifecycle Submitting A Task Example Tracking Task Status Checkpoints And Recovery Language Durable Streaming Common Mistakes Related Guides # Durable Task Execution Durable tasks are for long-running AI work that should not be treated like a single short request. For first-agent onboarding, start with [registered actions](/docs/first-agent-onboarding). `POST /v1/tasks/submit` is an advanced durable-workflow surface for callers that already know they need direct task definitions. It is not the default way to let an agent call business actions. Use them when the workload needs: - multiple steps - explicit state progression - bounded execution over time - records that remain inspectable after the task completes or fails This page explains the durable-task model in practical terms and keeps recovery claims aligned with current proof status. --- ## What Durable Tasks Add Compared with a short synchronous request, a durable task adds: - task identity - execution-state tracking across steps - checkpoint and WAL-oriented structures - follow-up inspection through task status and receipt-oriented workflows That makes durable tasks the right fit for longer-running governed work. ## How To Think About The Lifecycle The durable-task lifecycle is still Request -> Execute -> Verify: - **Request** submits the task definition - **Execute** runs the task step by step under boundaries - **Verify** inspects task status, execution outcome, and receipt-oriented records ## Submitting A Task bash POST /v1/tasks/submit Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Content-Type: application/json The product supports different submission shapes, but they all become one durable execution workflow underneath. Use an idempotency key. If a network timeout makes the outcome unclear, inspect the existing task before submitting the same logical operation again. ### Example json { "task_type": "agent_workflow", "task_definition": { "steps": [ { "step_index": 0, "model": "gpt-4.1-mini", "messages": [ ] }, { "step_index": 1, "model": "gpt-4.1-mini", "messages": [ ] } ] }, "idempotency_key": "report-q3-2026-run-1" } ## Tracking Task Status bash GET /v1/tasks/TASK_ID Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Typical statuses include: | Status | Meaning | |---|---| | `pending` | Awaiting runtime assignment | | `dispatched` | Assigned and executing | | `checkpointed` | Mid-execution with checkpoint state recorded | | `completed` | All steps finished successfully | | `failed` | Execution ended with a non-recoverable error | | `recovering` | Recovery hand

title: Error Codes
description: Complete reference for all error responses returned by the Igris API.
content: Error Codes Error Response Format Authentication Errors `unauthorized` (HTTP 401) `forbidden` (HTTP 403) Rate Limiting Errors `rate_limit_exceeded` (HTTP 429) Billing Errors `budget_exceeded` (HTTP 402) `payment_required` (HTTP 402) Resource Errors `not_found` (HTTP 404) `conflict` (HTTP 409) `unprocessable` (HTTP 422) Execution Errors `provider_unavailable` (HTTP 502) `execution_timeout` (HTTP 504) `capability_violation` (HTTP 403) Fleet Errors `instance_limit_exceeded` (HTTP 429) `instance_not_found` (HTTP 404) Server Errors `internal_error` (HTTP 500) `service_unavailable` (HTTP 503) Error Code Summary # Error Codes Complete reference for all error responses returned by the Igris API. --- ## Error Response Format All errors follow a consistent JSON format: json { "error": { "code": "error_code", "message": "Human-readable description of the error", "details": {} } } | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `code` | string | Machine-readable error identifier | | `message` | string | Human-readable description | | `details` | object | Optional additional context (varies by error) | --- ## Authentication Errors ### `unauthorized` (HTTP 401) The request is missing or has an invalid authentication credential. json { "error": { "code": "unauthorized", "message": "Invalid or expired API key" } } **Common causes:** - API key is incorrect or has been revoked - API key is missing from the `Authorization` header - API key format is invalid ### `forbidden` (HTTP 403) The authenticated account does not have permission to access this resource. json { "error": { "code": "forbidden", "message": "This feature requires the Horizon tier or higher", "details": { "required_tier": "horizon", "current_tier": "seed" } } } This commonly appears when a Seed tenant attempts to access Horizon-only features such as team access, advanced event search, or failure-path configuration. --- ## Rate Limiting Errors ### `rate_limit_exceeded` (HTTP 429) The request rate limit has been exceeded. json { "error": { "code": "rate_limit_exceeded", "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please retry after the window resets.", "details": { "retry_after": 23, "limit": 100, "window": "60s" } } } See [Rate Limiting](/docs/rate-limiting) for details on limits and backoff strategies. --- ## Billing Errors ### `budget_exceeded` (HTTP 402) The tenant's monthly budget has been exhausted. json { "error": { "code": "budget_exceeded", "message": "Monthly budget exceeded.
