title: Routing Engine
description: The routing engine is an advanced path-selection layer inside Igris execution, combining policy, health, trust, and strategy-specific selection logic.
content: Routing Engine What It Is What It Considers Strategy Layer Relationship To Other Controls Console And Inspection Proof Language Related Pages # Routing Engine The routing engine is an advanced path-selection layer inside Igris execution. Its job is to choose among the execution paths that remain allowed and usable after policy, health, and trust have already narrowed the field. This makes it important to advanced operators, but it should not be read as the primary product identity. --- ## What It Is At a simple level: text Request -> policy and boundary checks -> health and trust filters -> routing engine -> selected execution path That means the routing engine is not a standalone product story. It is one layer inside the broader Execute stage. ## What It Considers Depending on configuration, the engine may consider: - latency behavior - success or failure history - cost signals - availability - strategy-specific selection logic Different deployment modes may expose different routing behavior, but the core idea is the same: choose an execution path under governance, not by ad hoc client-side guessing. ## Strategy Layer Different strategy modes can exist on top of the engine, such as adaptive, cost-aware, or latency-aware selection. Those strategies are advanced operator tools and should be evaluated with workload-specific evidence rather than broad assumptions. ## Relationship To Other Controls The engine sits behind: - policy - health - trust - circuit-breaker state That ordering matters. Advanced path selection should not override the safety and governance layers that determine whether a path should even be considered. ## Console And Inspection Routing dashboards can help explain which path was chosen and why, but they should be treated as advanced execution diagnostics. They are useful after you already understand the main product model. ## Proof Language The routing engine is a real advanced control layer, but this page should not promise globally optimal provider choice, automatic savings, or universal reliability gains without evidence for the specific workload and environment. ## Related Pages - [Semantic Routing →](/docs/semantic-routing) - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination)

title: Execution Model
description: This page explains the Igris execution model as Request -> Execute -> Verify, with governed boundaries and signed records around the run.
content: Execution Model Request Execute Boundaries Verify Signed Records Deployment Modes Fit Under The Same Model What To Treat Carefully # Execution Model The Igris execution model is: 1. **Request** 2. **Execute** 3. **Verify** Everything else on this page is a more detailed explanation of those three stages. --- ## Request Request is how work enters Igris. That can be a registered action run, a durable task submission, or an MCP tool call. The key idea is consistency: the request enters one execution system, not a collection of unrelated product identities. At request time, Igris establishes the context that matters for the run: - identity and tenant scope - input payload and parameters - capability expectations - applicable limits or policy boundaries ## Execute Execution is where the request becomes governed work. During execution, Igris can: - apply capability and policy checks - enforce budgets and other boundaries - capture execution events and state - run on the hosted or runtime-backed path configured for the workload - record violations or failure outcomes instead of hiding them This is the layer that turns a plain model response into an inspectable run. ### Boundaries Typical execution boundaries include: | Boundary | What it restricts | |---|---| | Capability gates | What the run is allowed to do | | Token or resource limits | How much work the run can consume | | Time limits | How long execution is allowed to continue | | Tool restrictions | Which external actions are allowed | If execution exceeds an allowed boundary, that outcome should be recorded as part of the run. ## Verify Verification is how you inspect what happened after execution. Depending on the path, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt hashes - proof-status information That is what makes the system useful for review, governance, and post-run analysis. ## Signed Records The model is not complete until the run produces something you can inspect later. In Igris terms, that can include: - the execution envelope for the run context - the execution receipt for the final record - hash-linked receipt material for downstream audit workflows Use [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) and [Verification](/docs/verification) for the public-facing receipt and proof workflows. ## Deployment Modes Fit Under The Same Model Hosted, local, and hybrid setups all fit under the same execution model: - the request still enters through Igris - executio

title: Execution Receipts
description: Execution receipts are the customer-facing audit record for what ran, where it ran, and whether policy violations occurred.
content: Execution Receipts Current Query Surface What a Receipt Contains List Receipts Export Receipts Proof Verification # Execution Receipts Execution receipts are the customer-facing audit record for what ran, where it ran, and whether policy violations occurred. --- ## Current Query Surface The current customer query surface for receipts lives in Overture: - `GET /v1/receipts` - `GET /v1/receipts/:id` - `GET /v1/receipts/export` - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` The current runtime build does **not** expose a public local `GET /v1/receipts` listing endpoint. If you are running fully local, consume the signed `execution_receipt` data returned in responses and store it in your own workflow if you need local retention. ## What a Receipt Contains A receipt is a record of *what ran, where, and whether policy held* — not a copy of the data that flowed through the run. It carries safe execution metadata: identifiers, timings, resource counts, status, policy/violation flags, and integrity fields (hashes and a signature). It does not store raw request bodies, raw response bodies, or file contents. Where a short human-readable hint is included (such as a prompt preview), it is a truncated preview, not the full payload. Receipts and evidence reads are tenant-bound: you can only read records owned by your own tenant. --- ## List Receipts bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts?limit=50&violations_only=true" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Supported query parameters: | Parameter | Description | |---|---| | `limit` | Max results, default `50`, max `500` | | `from` | Inclusive lower timestamp bound | | `to` | Inclusive upper timestamp bound | | `agent_id` | Filter by agent ID | | `violations_only` | Restrict to violating executions | Current response shape: json [ { "execution_id": "exec-01HXYZ", "agent_id": "agent-abc", "runtime_id": "runtime-01", "tenant_id": "tenant-456", "timestamp_utc": "2026-03-01T12:00:00Z", "wall_time_ms": 312, "cpu_time_ms": 287, "memory_peak_mb": 48, "tool_calls": 1, "violation_occurred": false, "status": "completed", "receipt_hash": "sha256:a3f9...", "previous_hash": "sha256:b2e8...", "signature": "base64:...", "transaction_id": "txn-01HXYZ", "prompt_preview": "Evaluate whether to initiate..." } ] --- ## Export Receipts bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=jsonl&from=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -o receipts.jsonl The current export formats a

content: First Agent Onboarding 0. Install An Agent Template Required Values 1. Install The CLI 2. Install The Starter Action Pack 3. Run The First Action 4. Connect Claude Code With MCP 5. Use Codex, Cursor, Or Terminal Agents 6. Custom Agents Stop Conditions Related Guides # First Agent Onboarding Use this path when a real agent or MCP client needs to run its first Igris action. The fastest supported path is **templates-first**: install the CLI, generate an agent template, install the starter Action Pack, run one registered action with an idempotency key, then inspect the run and evidence. ## 0. Install An Agent Template Pick the template that matches your agent environment: bash igris templates list igris templates install claude-code # Claude Code MCP igris templates install codex # terminal / Codex-style agents igris templates install cursor # Cursor MCP or CLI fallback igris templates install custom-agent # REST or MCP for any agent Files land in `.igris/templates/ /` by default. Use `--print` to preview without writing files. Verify when credentials are ready: bash igris templates verify claude-code See [Agent Templates](/docs/agent-templates) for all options. Templates generate local config only — they use the same CLI, REST, and MCP execution path as the steps below. Do not start by sending raw execution graphs. `POST /v1/tasks/submit` is an advanced durable-task API for custom workflows; first agents should call registered actions through REST, CLI, or MCP. ## Required Values Set these locally. Do not print secret values in logs or support tickets. bash export IGRIS_API_URL="https://overture.igrisinertial.com" export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_..." export IGRIS_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY="starter-echo-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)" Run the readiness doctor before wiring the agent: bash ./scripts/igris_doctor.sh The doctor checks required env names, API reachability, API-key acceptance on safe endpoints, MCP `tools/list` when credentials are available, optional MCP config JSON, runtime install metadata, and optional local-runtime reachability. It never echoes the API key. ## 1. Install The CLI Install the Igris CLI (`igris` / `igris-runtime`) from your environment's installer, then verify the key: bash igris auth login --api-url "$IGRIS_API_URL" ## 2. Install The Starter Action Pack The starter pack registers three safe `mock_demo` actions. No external provider credentials are required. bash igris packs list --api-url "$IGRIS_API_URL" igris packs install starter --api-url "$IGRIS_API_URL" REST equivalents: bash curl -sS "$IGRIS_API_URL/v1/action-packs" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" curl -sS -X POST "$IGRIS_API_URL/v1/action-packs/

title: First Hosted Integration
description: Register an action, run it with an idempotency key, and inspect the durable run — the standard first integration with the hosted Igris API.
content: First Hosted Integration 1. Create A Tenant API Key 2. Register An Action 3. Run The Action 4. Inspect The Run Where To Go Next Common Mistakes Related Guides # First Hosted Integration Igris runs **registered actions**. Instead of letting an agent call provider and tool APIs directly, you register the action once — what it does, where it runs, and what policy governs it — and the agent calls that action through one stable endpoint. Igris handles policy, tenant-scoped idempotency, routing, recovery, and proof. The first integration is four steps: 1. Create a tenant API key 2. Register an action 3. Run the action with an idempotency key 4. Inspect the run --- ## 1. Create A Tenant API Key Create one tenant API key for the environment that will call the hosted API. Treat it like any other production secret and keep it in your standard secret store. - [Trial & Billing →](/docs/trial-billing) - [API Authentication →](/docs/api-reference/authentication) ## 2. Register An Action An action definition is the contract for what an agent may ask Igris to run. This example registers a webhook-backed action that sends an invoice through your billing system: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/actions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "send_invoice", "display_name": "Send invoice", "description": "Send an invoice to a customer through the billing webhook.", "target_type": "webhook", "target_url": "https://billing.example.com/hooks/igris", "policy_preset": "Safe automation" }' A few things worth knowing before you pick values: - `target_type` decides where the action runs: `webhook` and `hosted_api` call an HTTP target, `local_runtime` runs on a runtime you install in your own environment, and `mock_demo` is a safe demo target that never calls an external API. - `policy_preset` governs every run. `Human-gated` pauses each run for approval; `Read-only` and `Non-replayable` constrain what recovery may do. - The full field list is in the [Actions API reference →](/docs/api-reference/actions/post-v1-actions). ## 3. Run The Action Agents and services run the action by name. Send an `idempotency_key` whenever a retry could double-run real work — retries with the same key inside your tenant return the original run instead of running the action again: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/actions/send_invoice/run \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "input": , "idempotency_key": "invo

content: First Verified Run What This Run Proves Prerequisites Run The Demo What The Script Does What To Inspect What Is Proven Locally What Is Not Proven By This Demo Real Provider Mode # First Verified Run This page walks through the narrowest honest proof-backed path in the repo today. Use it when you want to see Igris do real execution work and return verification-ready artifacts, without assuming unproven provider, fallback, or robotics behavior. --- ## What This Run Proves The local proof demonstrates: - one request sent through Overture - execution handed off to Runtime - signed `execution_envelope` returned from the run - signed `execution_receipt` returned from the run - receipt hash recomputation and receipt-log chain verification - route-decision metadata showing the request was forwarded to Runtime This is a **proven locally** path based on the current proof artifacts. ## Prerequisites - A checkout of this repository - `node`, `go`, `cargo`, `curl`, and `lsof` - Free ports `8080` and `8081` - Free port `18090` for the default mock-provider mode ## Run The Demo From the repo root: bash ./scripts/unified_execution_proof_demo.sh Expected output shape: text Unified execution proof succeeded. Mode: mock Provider: local-mock-cloud Route decision: forwarded_to_runtime_task Receipt execution_id: ... Receipt hash: ... Artifacts: /tmp/igris-unified-proof.XXXXXX ## What The Script Does 1. Prepares local proof artifacts, including an offline license artifact and local signing material. 2. Builds or reuses the Runtime binary. 3. Builds the Overture binary. 4. Starts a local mock OpenAI-compatible upstream on `127.0.0.1:18090`. 5. Starts Runtime on `127.0.0.1:8080`. 6. Starts Overture on `127.0.0.1:8081`. 7. Sends one `/v1/infer` request through Overture. 8. Fails if Overture falls back away from Runtime. 9. Verifies the returned `execution_envelope`. 10. Verifies the returned `execution_receipt`, its hash, and its receipt-log chain entry. ## What To Inspect The script prints an artifact directory at the end of the run. The most useful files are: - `overture-response.json` for the public response payload - `verification.json` for the verification summary - `logs/overture.log` for handoff behavior - `logs/runtime.log` for runtime-side execution details ## What Is Proven Locally | Claim | Status | |---|---| | Unified Request -> Execute -> Verify flow through Overture and Runtime | Proven locally | | Signed execution envelope verification | Proven locally | | Signed execution receipt verification | Proven locally | | Receipt-hash verification | P

title: Fleet Management
description: Use fleet management to register, inspect, and coordinate execution environments that participate in Igris workflows.
content: Fleet Management 1. Register Execution Environments 2. Track Heartbeats And Coordination Surfaces 3. Inspect Registered Environments 4. Treat Config Push Carefully 5. Treat OTA-Style Updates Carefully What Fleet Management Means In Practice Common Mistakes Related Guides # Fleet Management Use fleet management when you need visibility into the execution environments that participate in Igris workflows. This page is about operating registered runtime environments. The reliable, practical use cases today are: - registering execution environments - monitoring whether they remain visible and healthy enough to participate - inspecting runtime coordination surfaces - using queued command and rollout features carefully --- ## 1. Register Execution Environments The stock runtime attempts registration automatically when both `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` are present at startup. If you are integrating a custom launcher, use the runtime registration contract: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/api/v1/runtime/register \ -H "X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "machine_id": "edge-gateway-01", "hostname": "edge-gateway-01", "platform": "linux-amd64", "runtime_version": "1.6.0", "endpoint": "http://192.168.1.100:8080", "public_key_ed25519": "YOUR_RUNTIME_PUBLIC_KEY", "timestamp_unix_ms": 1775283660000, "signature": "YOUR_RUNTIME_SIGNATURE" }' Registration is the first operator check: if the environment cannot register, it should not be treated as a participating execution surface yet. ## 2. Track Heartbeats And Coordination Surfaces The main runtime coordination routes are: - `POST /api/v1/runtime/heartbeat` - `DELETE /api/v1/runtime/deregister` - `GET /api/v1/runtime/commands` These are runtime-to-hosted coordination surfaces. They are useful for operator workflows and automation, not as general application endpoints. ## 3. Inspect Registered Environments Use the runtime governance summary when you want inventory and visibility: bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/execution/governance/runtimes \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Agents can read the same inventory through the MCP `list_runtimes` tool, which also reports whether each runtime is currently routable. title: Fleet Rollout Workflow
description: Use this workflow when you want to introduce Igris execution environments gradually and verify behavior before expanding rollout.
content: Fleet Rollout Workflow 1. Start With A Small Environment Set 2. Observe Execution Before Expanding 3. Roll Configuration Deliberately 4. Expand In Stages 5. Keep Rollback Simple Common Mistakes Related Guides # Fleet Rollout Workflow Use this workflow when you want to introduce runtime-backed execution environments in stages instead of turning on broad rollout all at once. The goal is simple: 1. start small 2. observe execution behavior 3. verify the records that matter 4. expand only after the first slice is stable This page is about staged rollout of execution environments. --- ## 1. Start With A Small Environment Set Before expanding rollout, make sure each target environment can: - start cleanly - register successfully - remain visible through heartbeat reporting - execute the workload shape you care about If those basics are not healthy, rollout is the wrong next step. ## 2. Observe Execution Before Expanding Do not treat rollout as a blind infrastructure action. Use the first slice to inspect: - whether environments stay registered - whether requests route the way you expect - whether execution events and receipts remain available - whether customer-facing traffic is unaffected This is the practical operator version of Request -> Execute -> Verify. ## 3. Roll Configuration Deliberately If you use config-push surfaces, separate configuration changes from binary updates whenever possible. That makes it easier to answer: - did the environment change break execution behavior - did the binary change introduce the issue - which step should be rolled back first Config-push surfaces exist, but broad rollout success should still be described carefully unless you have reproducible evidence for the exact pattern you are using. ## 4. Expand In Stages A safe rollout sequence looks like: 1. one environment or a small canary group 2. inspect runtime visibility and execution behavior 3. check receipts or proof-oriented inspection where the workflow depends on them 4. expand to the next slice only after the first slice is stable Avoid language that implies failover or recovery is already proven across the whole environment set. ## 5. title: Governance
description: Governance in Igris means applying boundaries, permissions, execution events, and signed records around the Request -> Execute -> Verify lifecycle.
content: Governance What Governance Covers Before Execution: Permissions And Scope During Execution: Boundaries And Events After Execution: Signed Records Capability Boundaries Review And Follow-Up What To Avoid Claiming Related Guides # Governance Governance in Igris starts with the Request -> Execute -> Verify model. - **Request** defines what work is being asked for and under which context. - **Execute** applies permissions, boundaries, and runtime checks while the work runs. - **Verify** makes the resulting events and signed records available for inspection later. This page is about the practical controls around execution, not about broad unsupported governance claims. --- ## What Governance Covers Governance answers four operator questions: 1. what was requested 2. what the run was allowed to do 3. what happened during execution 4. what record is available afterward That maps directly to: - permissions and capability checks - execution boundaries - execution events and outcome state - signed records and receipt-oriented inspection ## Before Execution: Permissions And Scope Before the main work runs, Igris can apply controls such as: - tenant or deployment scope - capability grants - allowed tools or access paths - duration or resource expectations This is the part of governance that decides whether the request is allowed to become execution at all. ## During Execution: Boundaries And Events While the run is active, governance is about keeping execution inside its declared boundaries and making the outcome inspectable. Examples include: - capability checks during tool or action attempts - resource boundaries such as duration or token limits - recording violations or rejected actions - surfacing execution events that help operators understand what happened That is why governance belongs to execution itself, not just to a static policy document. ## After Execution: Signed Records Governance is only useful if the result can be checked later. Depending on the path, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt-oriented audit records Use these pages for the public-facing workflow: - [Verification →](/docs/verification) - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status) ## Capability Boundaries Governance often starts with capability scope. description: Use this workflow when one Igris execution model needs to span hosted coordination and local runtime execution.
content: Hybrid Deployment Workflow 1. Keep One Application-Facing Contract 2. Start Runtimes With The Right Registration Context 3. Verify Hosted And Runtime Health Separately 4. Decide What Must Stay Hosted Versus Local 5. Treat Failure Paths Carefully Common Mistakes Related Guides # Hybrid Deployment Workflow Use this workflow when one Igris execution model needs to span hosted and local environments. Hybrid deployment is still one product story: - **Request** enters through a stable application-facing Igris surface - **Execute** can involve hosted coordination and runtime-backed execution - **Verify** stays tied to the same records, receipts, and inspection workflows This model is useful when you care about: - governance across hosted and local environments - running execution closer to devices or private infrastructure - clearer failure-path handling between application traffic and runtime operations - verification-ready records even when execution topology is mixed --- ## 1. Keep One Application-Facing Contract In most hybrid setups, the application still points at the hosted base URL: text https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1 That keeps the application contract stable while allowing runtime participation underneath. ## 2. Start Runtimes With The Right Registration Context Hybrid deployment only works when the runtime can start and register correctly. bash export IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY="YOUR_LICENSE_KEY" export IGRIS_API_KEY="YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" igris-runtime serve This is the operational step that makes runtime-backed participation possible. It does not create a second product surface for the application team. ## 3. Verify Hosted And Runtime Health Separately Check both sides of the system deliberately: - hosted API calls succeed with your tenant API key - the runtime answers `http://localhost:8080/v1/health` - runtime registration and visibility succeed where your workflow depends on them Hybrid works best when execution traffic and runtime operations are both observable. ## 4. Decide What Must Stay Hosted Versus Local Use hosted coordination when you want: - the simplest application-facing entry path - provider-backed execution without device-local routing decisions in the client - centralized operator workflows Use runtime-backed execution when you want: - locality - device-level governance - execution near private infrastructure or tools The important point is that the workflow still belongs to one execution system. ## 5. title: Identity & Access
description: How Igris handles console identity, tenant API keys, tenant roles, and higher-assurance access controls.
content: Identity & Access Two Access Planes Console Identity Tenant API Keys Tenant Roles Higher-Assurance Access Controls 2FA SSO Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Identity & Access Igris separates **human access** from **programmatic access**. - **Console identity** is for people using the web app - **Tenant API keys** are for applications, automation, and deployed runtimes Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Two Access Planes | Plane | Used by | Primary credential | Scope | |---|---|---|---| | **Console** | Human operators | Session cookie | Browser session tied to a tenant user | | **API** | Apps, agents, runtimes | `igris_` API key | Tenant-scoped machine access | Console cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. For scripts and integrations, use tenant API keys. --- ## Console Identity The console uses a session-based sign-in model. A user signs in once, receives a session cookie, and then operates inside one tenant context at a time. Current product behavior: - Console access is designed for interactive human use - Session state is separate from tenant API-key auth - Tenant context is applied before policy, billing, and audit logic This keeps browser access and machine access cleanly separated. --- ## Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys are the automation contract for the coordination layer. Accepted forms: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Use tenant API keys for: - server-side application calls - CI/CD or operational automation - provisioning and runtime registration flows - customer-visible integrations that should not depend on browser cookies Do not reuse one tenant's API key across other tenants. Keys are tenant-scoped by design. --- ## Tenant Roles Igris distinguishes between ordinary tenant access and elevated administrative access. In practical terms, roles matter for: - tenant administration - sensitive configuration changes - identity and security operations - management actions that should not be available to every authenticated caller When you design operational workflows, treat roles as part of the product boundary that customers and operators can reason about directly. --- ## Higher-Assurance Access Controls Igris includes stronger access controls for deployments that need more than basic session auth plus API keys. ### 2FA Two-factor authentication is available for tenant-level console access hardening. Use it when console operators can perform security-sensitive actions such as reviewing paused executions, rotating provider keys, or chang

title: Install
description: Install the Igris CLI and run the first Run / Recover / Prove demo without Postgres, Docker, or a repository checkout.
content: Install First Run Uninstall Security Notes Advanced Validation # Install Run the public installer: bash curl -fsSL https://igrisinertial.com/install | bash The installer detects macOS/Linux and arm64/x86_64, downloads the matching CLI archive, verifies the checksum when release checksum metadata is published, and installs into `~/.igris/bin`. It does not use `sudo` and does not silently edit shell profiles. If `~/.igris/bin` is not on your `PATH`, add it explicitly: bash export PATH="$HOME/.igris/bin:$PATH" ## First Run bash igris doctor igris demo --recover-prove The demo is self-contained. It does not require Postgres, Docker, Homebrew Postgres, provider credentials, runtime key setup, or a cloned repository. Expected output includes: text Action requested: read-only task Policy applied: ... Runtime boundary recorded: ... Recovery demo: irreversible replay blocked Receipt verification: verified Open the execution story: file://... The first-run proof is demo evidence. It uses a generated local runtime key and a signed receipt so you can see the Run / Recover / Prove model immediately. It is not a production deployment claim. ## Uninstall bash igris uninstall rm -rf "$HOME/.igris" Remove any `PATH` line you added to your shell profile. ## Security Notes - The installer is readable shell served from `https://igrisinertial.com/install`. - Installation is user-local by default: `~/.igris/bin`. - Checksums are verified when published for the selected artifact. - No telemetry is collected by the installer or first-run demo. - Do not paste private keys, tokens, raw callback bodies, database credentials, or environment secrets into support tickets or public transcripts. ## Advanced Validation Contributors who want the full advanced local validation path can still use: bash make run-recover-prove-local-provision That advanced path can use Homebrew/manual Postgres or optional Docker. It is separate from the first-run installer demo.

title: Key Management
description: Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer.
content: Key Management What The Current Public API Supports Add A Provider Key Rotate, Validate, Remove Security Properties # Key Management Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer. --- ## What The Current Public API Supports The current public vault API accepts these provider identifiers: | Provider | Intended use | |---|---| | `openai` | Customer cloud traffic | | `anthropic` | Customer cloud traffic | | `benchmark` | Synthetic or test traffic | Do not assume broader provider coverage on the public vault API unless it is explicitly documented in the current contract. --- ## Add A Provider Key bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' Current request fields: | Field | Description | |---|---| | `provider` | Provider identifier such as `openai` | | `key_name` | Human-readable name for the key | | `api_key` | Provider secret to encrypt and store | --- ## Rotate, Validate, Remove Current routes: - `GET /v1/vault/keys` - `GET /v1/vault/keys/:provider` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/rotate` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/validate` - `DELETE /v1/vault/keys/:provider` The current response contract returns masked values only. Raw provider secrets are never returned after creation. --- ## Security Properties - Provider keys are encrypted before storage - Key operations are tenant-scoped - API responses expose masked key material only - Vault operations are available through authenticated control-plane APIs --- [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) · [Security →](/docs/security) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

title: Licensing & Activation
description: How Igris licenses are activated, validated, and kept alive across the console, coordination layer, and deployed runtimes.
content: Licensing & Activation Product Model Tenant Activation Runtime Admission Device Identity And Heartbeats What The License Controls Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Licensing & Activation Igris licensing is not just a billing flag. It is part of the runtime bootstrap path. There are two distinct surfaces: - **Tenant activation in the console** associates a purchased license with a tenant - **Runtime validation and heartbeat** determine whether a deployed runtime is allowed to stay active Treat those as one lifecycle. --- ## Product Model At a high level, the licensing flow works like this: 1. A tenant activates a license key from the console. 2. The runtime validates that license during startup. 3. The runtime registers a device identity under that license. 4. The runtime sends periodic heartbeats to remain counted as active. If validation fails, the runtime should not be treated as fully admitted into the platform. --- ## Tenant Activation The console exposes a tenant-facing activation flow so an operator can bind a license to the current tenant account. From a product perspective, that does three things: - sets the active plan for the tenant - determines the feature set and quota envelope - establishes the license record that runtimes will validate against The console also exposes plan and quota state, including: - current plan - license status - request quota - device quota - active device count That means licensing is visible to both finance and operations, not just procurement. --- ## Runtime Admission The runtime performs license validation during startup before it proceeds with its normal cloud-registration path. In practical terms, runtime admission depends on: - a valid license key - a generated device identity - the runtime version reported during validation The runtime then attempts device registration under that license. This is important operationally because a license is not only "valid" or "invalid"; it also tracks how many active devices are attached to it. --- ## Device Identity And Heartbeats Each runtime derives a device ID from local machine characteristics and registers that device against the license. Once registered, the runtime sends periodic heartbeats. This gives Igris an operational answer to questions like: - which runtimes are still alive - how many devices are currently consuming the license - whether a device should be treated as stale or deregistered If you are operating a fleet, heartbeats are part of capacity accounting, not just health reporting. --- ## What The License Controls Lice

title: Local LLM Fallback
description: igris-runtime can serve GGUF models locally and participate in hybrid deployments where cloud routing falls back to on-device inference.
content: Local LLM Fallback What Exists Today Configuration Fields Hybrid Behavior Supported Model Format Operational Notes # Local LLM Fallback `igris-runtime` can serve GGUF models locally and participate in hybrid deployments where cloud routing falls back to on-device inference. --- ## What Exists Today The current runtime config surface is `local_fallback`. The shipped config supports local model loading and tuning knobs such as context size, threading, GPU layer offload, and prompt caching. json5 { local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/mistral-7b.Q4_K_M.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0, max_tokens: 512, temperature: 0.7 } } Optional fields also available in the current runtime: - `main_gpu` - `prompt_cache_dir` - `batch_size` - `lora_adapter_path` --- ## Configuration Fields | Field | Description | |---|---| | `enabled` | Enables the local fallback subsystem | | `model_path` | Path to the GGUF model on disk | | `context_size` | Runtime context window size | | `threads` | CPU threads for local inference | | `n_gpu_layers` | Number of model layers offloaded to GPU | | `max_tokens` | Default local generation cap | | `temperature` | Default local sampling temperature | There is no dedicated pure-local fallback toggle in the current runtime config. For pure local deployments, point clients directly at `http://localhost:8080/v1` and do not rely on cloud routing. --- ## Hybrid Behavior In a hybrid deployment: 1. Your application calls Overture 2. Overture routes normally across cloud providers 3. If the runtime is registered and selected by your routing configuration, local execution can participate in the request path In a fully local deployment: 1. Your application calls the runtime directly 2. The runtime answers from the local model 3. Signed execution receipts are returned with the response payload when enabled by the runtime path --- ## Supported Model Format The current runtime expects GGUF model files on disk. content: MCP Guide Pages Transport Surface How MCP Fits In # MCP MCP is the agent-facing control surface in Igris. An agent connects to one endpoint (`POST /v1/mcp`) and, scoped to its tenant, can do four things: - discover the **registered actions** it is allowed to call - call a registered action - inspect the resulting runs and their proof state - list the tenant's registered runtimes It is a narrow, strict-schema JSON-RPC surface — not a general-purpose context or resource store. The available tools are fixed (`list_actions`, `get_action`, `call_action`, `list_runs`, `get_run`, `get_run_evidence`, `list_runtimes`), every tool schema is closed (`additionalProperties: false`), and unknown fields are rejected. The tenant always comes from the credential and cannot be overridden through arguments. ## Guide Pages - [First Agent Onboarding](/docs/first-agent-onboarding): connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or a custom agent to registered actions - [MCP Server](/docs/mcp-server): the transport, the tool list, and strict-schema behavior - [MCP Integration Patterns](/docs/mcp-integration-patterns): durable, auditable patterns for calling actions and inspecting runs - [MCP Swarm Mode](/docs/mcp-swarm): multi-runtime context exchange (technical preview) ## Transport Surface - [`POST /v1/mcp`](/docs/mcp-server): JSON-RPC `tools/list` and `tools/call` ## How MCP Fits In Use MCP to let an agent call your registered actions and read back what happened. Use [durable tasks](/docs/durable-tasks) when long-running progress and recovery matter. Use [receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) for audit evidence. Keeping those three concerns separate is what keeps the system understandable at scale. --- [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) · [Integration Patterns →](/docs/mcp-integration-patterns) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

title: MCP Integration Patterns
description: Practical patterns for using the agent-facing MCP surface to call registered actions and inspect runs in production.
content: MCP Integration Patterns Pattern: Call Registered Actions, Not Inline Graphs Pattern: Make Every Call Idempotent Pattern: Acknowledge, Then Inspect Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Pattern: Confirm a Runtime Before Local Actions Related Guides # MCP Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use the [MCP server](/docs/mcp-server) as part of a production integration. MCP in Igris is an action/run control surface — these patterns are about calling registered actions safely and inspecting what happened, not about storing shared state. --- ## Pattern: Call Registered Actions, Not Inline Graphs `call_action` runs an action you have already registered. The action definition owns the target, policy, and approval behavior; the agent only supplies `input`. Do this when you want agents to act through a reviewed, named contract rather than constructing raw execution details at call time. The strict schema enforces this — the agent supplies inputs to a registered action and cannot inject execution internals through MCP. ## Pattern: Make Every Call Idempotent Pass an `idempotency_key` on `call_action`. Idempotency is tenant-scoped: a repeated key from the same tenant returns the existing run instead of starting a second one. Choose a key that is stable for the logical operation (for example, a ticket ID or a date-stamped job name), so an agent retry after a timeout does not double-run the action. ## Pattern: Acknowledge, Then Inspect `call_action` returns a `run_id` and an `inspect_ref` — it acknowledges acceptance, not completion. Confirm the outcome with `get_run`, and pull audit metadata with `get_run_evidence`. Do not treat the acknowledgement as proof the work finished. ## Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Keep transient prompt/working state in your own application. Use `get_run_evidence` and [receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) when you need the durable audit record. Evidence records carry safe metadata, not raw request or response bodies — do not expect MCP to hand back full payloads. ## Pattern: Confirm a Runtime Before Local Actions If an action targets a local runtime, `call_action` is refused unless the tenant has a healthy, reachable runtime connected. Use `list_runtimes` to confirm one is present and routable before driving local-runtime actions from an agent. See [Deploy Local Runtime](/docs/deploy-local-runtime) for the reachability requirement. ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Durable Tasks →](/docs/durable-tasks) - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts)

title: MCP Server
description: The agent-facing MCP endpoint exposes a fixed set of strict-schema tools for listing and calling registered actions and inspecting runs.
content: MCP Server Transport Tools Schemas Are Strict Calling an Action Inspecting Runs Integration Guidance Related Guides # MCP Server `POST /v1/mcp` is the agent-facing MCP endpoint. It is backed directly by Igris's action, task, and runtime primitives — it is not a generic context store and it does not forward arbitrary methods to a runtime. Treat it as a narrow, tenant-scoped control surface: an agent can discover the registered actions it is allowed to call, call them, and inspect the resulting runs and evidence. Nothing else is exposed. --- ## Transport The endpoint speaks JSON-RPC 2.0. Authentication is a tenant credential (BetterAuth); every call is scoped to the caller's tenant. Two methods are supported: - `tools/list` — return the available tools and their input schemas - `tools/call` — invoke a tool by name with `arguments` json { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": "req_1", "method": "tools/list", "params": {} } ## Tools The server exposes exactly these tools. There are no `context/*` or `resource/*` methods. | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `list_actions` | List the tenant's registered actions | | `get_action` | Fetch one registered action by `action_id` or `action_name` | | `call_action` | Run a registered action | | `list_runs` | List recent runs for the tenant | | `get_run` | Fetch one run's status and proof state | | `get_run_evidence` | Fetch a run's evidence/receipt metadata | | `list_runtimes` | List the tenant's registered runtimes | ## Schemas Are Strict Every tool schema is closed: `additionalProperties` is `false`. Unknown fields are rejected rather than ignored. If you send a field a tool does not declare, the call fails with a validation error — so send only the documented arguments. The tenant is always taken from your credential. There is no argument you can add to target another tenant or to bypass an action's configured target and policy; such fields are refused. ## Calling an Action `call_action` runs a **registered** action. You identify it by `action_id` or `action_name` (one is required); you cannot describe an arbitrary execution graph inline. The action definition decides the target and policy; your arguments only supply `input`, optional `metadata`, an `idempotency_key`, and an optional `deadline_at`. json { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": "req_2", "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "call_action", "arguments": { "action_name": "create_ticket", "input": , "idempotency_key": "node7-disk-2026-06-10" } } } If the action targets a local runtime, the call is r

title: MCP Swarm Mode
description: MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network.
content: MCP Swarm Mode What It Solves Operational Model Configuration Design Boundaries Common Mistakes Related Guides # MCP Swarm Mode MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network. Use it when context must move between devices or runtime instances without turning every exchange into an application-managed synchronization problem. --- ## What It Solves Swarm Mode is useful when: - multiple runtimes need the same operational context - one runtime should be able to continue after another runtime wrote the latest shared state - distributed planning or robotics coordination needs a shared context layer ## Operational Model In Swarm Mode: - runtimes discover peers - shared context is replicated across the swarm - reads can be served from a peer that did not originate the write That makes Swarm Mode a context-sharing mechanism, not a replacement for durable workflow recovery or audit evidence. ## Configuration toml [mcp_swarm] enabled = true discovery = "mdns" encryption_key_path = "/path/to/swarm.key" ## Design Boundaries Use Swarm Mode for shared operational state. Do not use it for: - signed audit records - long-term business data retention - progress recovery that should be modeled as a durable task ## Common Mistakes - treating swarm replication as if it were a durable checkpoint protocol - storing too much request-local prompt state in the shared swarm context - using swarm state where one runtime-local value would be simpler ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

description: Igris supports three memory systems: vector store for semantic retrieval, KV cache for fast key-value lookup, and cross-instance context via MCP Swarm Mode.

It gives agents access to a long-term knowledge base without including everything in the context window. **How it works:** 1. Documents are embedded and stored in the local vector index 2. At query time, the agent provides a query string 3. The vector store returns the top-K most similar documents 4. Retrieved documents are injected into the agent's context **Configuration:** json { "memory": { "vector_store": { "enabled": true, "top_k": 5, "similarity_threshold": 0.75 } } } **Supported embedding models:** - Any GGUF-format embedding model - External embedding APIs (via the HTTP tool) The vector index is stored on device. Embeddings do not leave the device unless you configure an external embedding endpoint. --- ## KV Cache The KV cache provides fast key-value storage for agent state that must persist across steps or across executions. **Use cases:** - Storing intermediate results between planning steps - Persisting agent state across tool calls - Caching frequently accessed data to reduce tool call latency **Access:** json { "kv_cache": { "set": }, "get": , "ttl_seconds": 3600 } } KV entries expire after `ttl_seconds`. The cache is local to the engine instance unless MCP Swarm Mode is enabled. --- ## Cross-Instance Context (MCP Swarm Mode) MCP Swarm Mode enables execution context to be shared across multiple engine instances. title: Model Aggregation (Technical Preview)
description: A preview-oriented look at model aggregation and federated-style learning workflows under Igris.
content: Model Aggregation (Technical Preview) What This Page Covers What Is Confirmed Today What Is Not Proven Here When To Evaluate It Related Pages # Model Aggregation (Technical Preview) Model aggregation is a specialized, preview-oriented surface in Igris. It is not part of the default Request -> Execute -> Verify path, and it should not be treated as a proof-backed production capability today. See [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before planning around this page. --- ## What This Page Covers In the codebase, Igris includes source-confirmed structures for federated-style learning workflows where multiple configured execution environments contribute updates to a shared model-improvement process. The high-level idea is: 1. local environments produce model-adaptation artifacts 2. those artifacts are collected centrally 3. an aggregated result is redistributed That is useful for organizations exploring privacy-preserving adaptation workflows, but the public proof for this area is still limited. --- ## What Is Confirmed Today - source-confirmed configuration and API surfaces exist for model-aggregation-style workflows - the idea fits naturally with hosted and hybrid deployment modes - operators can reason about this as a specialized execution-environment workflow rather than a separate product --- ## What Is Not Proven Here - end-to-end production model aggregation across real customer environments - public proof for privacy guarantees or convergence behavior - rollout guidance strong enough to treat this as generally available For those reasons, this page should be read as technical preview guidance, not a deployment commitment. --- ## When To Evaluate It Evaluate model aggregation only if you already need: - local adaptation close to where work happens - coordination across multiple configured execution environments - stronger control over what data leaves the execution surface If your immediate goal is governed execution with signed records and verification-ready receipts, start with the standard docs path instead. --- ## Related Pages - [Deployment →](/docs/deployment) - [Fleet Management →](/docs/fleet-management) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status)

Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail. --- ## Architecture Multi-tenancy in Igris is enforced at every layer: ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer │ │ │ │ Tenant A │ Tenant B │ │ Tenant C │ Tenant D │ └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ Runtime A │ │ Runtime B │ │ Runtime C │ │ (Tenant A) │ │ (Tenant B) │ │ (Tenant C) │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ ### Isolation guarantees | Layer | Isolation method | |---|---| | **Inference** | Separate API keys, separate provider configurations | | **Execution** | Separate execution envelopes with tenant-scoped IDs | | **Data** | Tenant-scoped storage — no cross-tenant data access | | **Policies** | Per-tenant policy envelopes | | **Audit** | Per-tenant receipt chains | | **Keys** | Per-tenant vault — keys are never shared | --- ## Tenant Identification Every request is associated with a tenant via the API key used for authentication. The API key maps to exactly one tenant. There is no cross-tenant key. API Key → Tenant ID → Execution Context The tenant ID is embedded in every execution receipt, ensuring full traceability from receipt back to tenant. --- ## Tenant Configuration Each tenant has an independent configuration: json { "tenant": { "id": "tenant-abc123", "name": "Acme Corp", "tier": "horizon", "providers": ["anthropic", "openai"], "policy": { "max_tokens": 4096, "max_steps": 10, "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false }, "slo": { "latency_p99_ms": 2000, "max_cost_per_request_usd": 0.05 } } } --- ## Resource Quotas Tenants are allocated resource quotas based on their tier: | Resource | Seed | Horizon | Infinite | |---|---|---|---| | Projects | 1 | 5 | Custom | | Execution environments | 1 | 10 | Custom | | Verified runs / month | 2,500 | 50,000 | Custom | | Receipt retention | 7 days | 60 days | Custom retention policy | | Team access | — | ✓ | ✓ | | Advanced event search | — | ✓ | ✓ | | Private deployment options | — | — | ✓ | When a tenant exceeds its quota, requests are rejected with HTTP 429. The `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header indicates remaining capacity. --- ## Cross-Tenant Isolation ### Data isolation - Execution receipts are scoped to tenant — no tenant

title: Observability & Tracing
description: How Igris exposes request lineage, trace IDs, and distributed tracing across the coordination layer and runtime.
content: Observability & Tracing Trace Identity Distributed Tracing What Operators Should Expect Relationship To Receipts Recommended Deployment Model Related Pages # Observability & Tracing Igris has two observability layers: - **product-visible lineage** such as request IDs, receipts, and execution history - **operator-visible tracing** such as spans, trace propagation, and deployment telemetry You need both. Receipts tell you what happened. Tracing tells you where time was spent and where a request crossed system boundaries. --- ## Trace Identity The coordination layer generates and propagates a trace identity for each request. That identity is attached to logs and returned through `X-Trace-ID` so operators can correlate: - inbound API traffic - routing decisions - provider calls - runtime handoff - receipt and audit records From a product perspective, `X-Trace-ID` is the fast path for debugging cross-system behavior. --- ## Distributed Tracing Igris supports OpenTelemetry-style tracing with a Jaeger exporter and request-scoped trace attributes. That combination matters because Igris needs to support both: - cross-service span propagation - external tracing systems used by platform teams Current tracing metadata can include things like: - HTTP method and path - provider and model - token counts - latency and cost - advanced path-selection metadata when those features are enabled This makes tracing useful for routing analysis, not just generic HTTP timing. --- ## What Operators Should Expect Tracing should answer these questions quickly: - Did the request stay in cloud or move to runtime? - Which provider was selected and why? - Where did latency accumulate? - Was an advanced path-selection feature involved? - Is a slow request caused by routing, provider latency, or local runtime work? That is the difference between basic logging and a usable production observability model. --- ## Relationship To Receipts Tracing and receipts are related but not interchangeable. | Surface | Primary use | |---|---| | **Trace ID / spans** | live debugging, latency analysis, request-path inspection | | **Execution receipt** | tamper-evident record of the governed execution outcome | Use tracing when you are diagnosing behavior in-flight. Use receipts when you need durable audit evidence. --- ## Recommended Deployment Model For production environments: - return or capture `X-Trace-ID` in client and operator tooling - export traces to your tracing system - correlate traces with execution receipts and request IDs - retain tracing for opera

title: Provider Health
description: Provider health is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism for failure-aware path selection during execution.
content: Provider Health What Provider Health Means Health States Why It Matters How It Affects Execution Monitoring Surfaces Proof Language Related Pages # Provider Health Provider health is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism inside the **Execute** stage. Its purpose is straightforward: help Igris avoid obviously unhealthy upstream paths and make failure-aware execution decisions. This page is about the mechanics of that decision support, not about turning routing into the product identity. --- ## What Provider Health Means Provider health asks whether a configured upstream path appears usable right now. Typical signals include: - response success or failure - latency behavior - recent throughput - health-check outcomes where those are enabled These signals help path selection, but they do not guarantee a perfect execution outcome. ## Health States The exact thresholds depend on configuration, but the common states are: - **active** when the path looks healthy enough to use normally - **degraded** when the path is still available but should be treated more cautiously - **unavailable** when the path should not receive ordinary execution traffic This is about failure visibility and safer path selection, not a blanket survival promise. ## Why It Matters Provider health helps operators answer: - which upstream paths are currently usable - whether a sudden latency or error spike should reduce traffic - whether a path should be removed from ordinary selection until it recovers That makes it part of governed execution rather than just a dashboard nicety. ## How It Affects Execution Provider health feeds into hosted path selection alongside: - policy - trust - circuit-breaker state - any advanced routing mode in use Health should narrow the set of usable paths before an advanced routing strategy makes its final choice. ## Monitoring Surfaces Use the health APIs and console views to inspect health state, but keep expectations realistic: - health telemetry helps explain execution behavior - health telemetry does not by itself prove performance or reliability outcomes for every workload ## Proof Language Provider health is an advanced execution mechanism with real implementation support. It is appropriate to describe it as failure-aware path selection, but not as a guarantee that every outage or degradation scenario is already solved automatically. ## Related Pages - [Provider Trust →](/docs/provider-trust) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [Cloud Coordination

title: Provider Trust
description: Provider trust is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism for deciding whether an available path should still be considered reliable enough for execution.
content: Provider Trust What Trust Evaluates Why It Matters Cold Start And Confidence How It Affects Path Selection Proof Language Related Pages # Provider Trust Provider trust is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism. Health asks whether a path appears up right now. Trust asks whether that path should still be considered reliable enough to keep using for governed execution. That distinction matters for advanced operators who want more than a binary up-or-down signal. --- ## What Trust Evaluates Trust looks at observed behavior over time, such as: - latency drift - error-rate drift - cost drift - how much evidence exists for the path so far This helps distinguish "technically available" from "credible enough to keep using." ## Why It Matters A path can be healthy in the narrow sense and still be a poor choice if its behavior is drifting away from what operators expect. Trust is the layer that says: - this path is up, but not yet proven enough - this path is up, but its behavior has drifted too far - this path may need more evidence before it receives normal traffic ## Cold Start And Confidence Trust grows with evidence. New or rarely used paths may need a warm-up period before operators should treat them as ordinary choices for production execution. That is part of the point of having a separate trust concept. ## How It Affects Path Selection Trust should sit ahead of final advanced routing decisions: 1. policy decides what is allowed 2. health decides what is currently usable 3. trust decides what is credible enough to keep using 4. final path selection chooses among the remaining candidates ## Proof Language Provider trust is best described as an advanced, source-confirmed execution mechanism. It is appropriate to explain how it influences selection, but this page should not promise globally optimal or universally safer outcomes without deployment-specific evidence. ## Related Pages - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [SLO Enforcer →](/docs/slo-enforcer)

title: Rate Limiting
description: The hosted API applies a global rate limit of 100 requests per minute by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated 10 downloads per hour per tenant cap.
content: Rate Limiting What The Hosted API Enforces 429 Response Shape Runtime Download Limit Local Runtime Rate Limits Client Guidance # Rate Limiting The hosted API applies a global rate limit of **100 requests per minute** by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated **10 downloads per hour per tenant** cap. --- ## What The Hosted API Enforces The hosted API applies: - one shared window: `100 req/min` by default - scoped per tenant when tenant context exists, otherwise per IP The hosted API does **not** publish rate-limit headers on every successful response. Rate-limit headers are guaranteed on rejection responses. --- ## 429 Response Shape When the global limiter is exceeded, the current response looks like this: json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } Headers on the rejection path include: - `Retry-After` - `X-RateLimit-Limit` - `X-RateLimit-Remaining` Do not depend on `X-RateLimit-Reset` being present on successful requests in the current build. --- ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime archive downloads have a separate limit of `10/hour` per tenant on the control plane download surface. This applies to: - `GET /v1/runtime/download` - subscribed runtime download workflows behind the cloud control plane --- ## Local Runtime Rate Limits The local runtime auth config supports its own request controls: json5 { auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY", rate_limit_per_minute: 60, rate_limit_burst: 10 } } | Field | Description | |---|---| | `rate_limit_per_minute` | Maximum local requests per minute | | `rate_limit_burst` | Additional local burst budget | --- ## Client Guidance - Treat `429` plus `retry_after_seconds` as the contract - Add exponential backoff client-side - Batch receipt exports and large history queries - Do not assume tier-specific global limits unless they are explicitly published in a future release contract --- [Troubleshooting →](/docs/troubleshooting) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

title: Receipts and Audit Workflow
description: Use this workflow when you need signed records, verification-ready receipts, or exportable audit evidence.
content: Receipts and Audit Workflow 1. Run Through A Documented Igris Surface 2. Inspect The Execution Outcome 3. Retrieve The Receipt-Oriented Record 4. Verify With The Right Expectation 5. Retain Or Export The Record Common Mistakes Related Guides # Receipts and Audit Workflow Use this workflow when a run needs to be inspected, verified, and retained after execution. The practical sequence is: 1. run through a documented Igris surface 2. inspect the execution outcome 3. retrieve the receipt-oriented record 4. verify what can actually be checked 5. retain or export the result for downstream use --- ## 1. Run Through A Documented Igris Surface Receipts are most useful when the request goes through a documented Igris path. Keep integrations on supported surfaces so execution metadata, receipts, and export workflows line up with the actual run. ## 2. Inspect The Execution Outcome Start with the immediate execution result: - response content - execution metadata - route decision or provider label where applicable This tells you what happened during the run. It is useful for debugging and operational review, but it is not the same thing as the receipt itself. ## 3. Retrieve The Receipt-Oriented Record Use receipt listing and detail endpoints when you need the signed or hash-linked execution record. - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) Treat the receipt surface as the audit artifact. Treat execution history as supporting context, not as a substitute for the receipt. ## 4. Verify With The Right Expectation Use the strongest verification surface that matches your need. For the narrow proof-backed path today: - the local verified run proves signature checks, receipt-hash checks, and receipt-log chain checks - see [First Verified Run](/docs/first-verified-run) For the hosted proof route: - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` compares submitted receipt values against the stored record and returns proof-status information - it should be described as stored-value comparison and proof-status sync, not as a full public cryptographic verifier See [Verification](/docs/verification) for the distinction. ## 5. Retain Or Export The Record Use `GET /v1/receipts/export` when another system, reviewer, or audit process needs the record outside the immediate execution flow. Choose: - NDJSON for machine pipelines - CSV for spreadsheet-oriented workflows Decide on retention and downstream custody before exporting receipts into another system. ## Common Mistakes - Treating execution history as if it were the signed receipt - Describing the hosted proof route as stronger than it is

title: Request -> Execute -> Verify
description: The core Igris mental model: send one request, govern execution, and inspect the records that come back.
content: Request -> Execute -> Verify Request Execute Verify Why This Model Matters What This Page Does Not Assume # Request -> Execute -> Verify Igris is easiest to understand as one execution system for AI tasks. Instead of thinking in terms of "hosted product versus local product," start with the lifecycle of the work: 1. **Request** 2. **Execute** 3. **Verify** --- ## Request Request means you submit work through an Igris API surface. That can be: - a registered action run (`POST /v1/actions/:name/run`) - a durable task submission or an MCP tool call - a runtime or operator workflow that still produces execution records The point is consistency. Your application should not need a different mental model every time the execution path changes. ## Execute Execution is where Igris earns its keep. During execution, Igris can: - route work to the configured hosted or runtime path - apply capability and policy boundaries - capture execution metadata and events - surface failure paths instead of hiding them - return signed execution material alongside the result Execution is not just "a provider responded." It is the governed run that happened between the request and the final response. ## Verify Verification means you can inspect what happened after the run. Depending on the path, that can include: - route-decision metadata - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt hashes and chain-linked log material This is what makes Igris useful for production work that needs review, audit, or post-run debugging. ## Why This Model Matters Direct provider calls are fine when all you need is a text response. Igris is for the point where the output starts doing real work and you care about: - governance - visible failure handling - post-run inspection - records that can be checked later ## What This Page Does Not Assume This model does **not** assume that every advanced feature is already proven in your environment. Real-provider execution, local GGUF fallback, checkpoint recovery, fleet failover, robotics, and multimodal flows all have their own proof status and should be evaluated explicitly. --- [Quick Start →](/docs/quickstart) · [Verification →](/docs/verification) · [Architecture →](/docs/architecture)

title: Safety & Containment
description: Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed.
content: Safety & Containment Containment Model Resource limits cgroup bounds (Linux) Capability Enforcement Secure Defaults Violation Handling Human-in-the-Loop # Safety & Containment Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. --- ## Containment Model Every execution runs in a containment context. The containment context applies resource limits before the model is invoked and enforces them throughout execution. ### Resource limits Limits are applied per-execution: | Limit | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `max_tokens` | 4096 | Maximum output tokens | | `max_duration_ms` | 30000 | Maximum wall time (30s) | | `max_steps` | 10 | Maximum tool/planning steps | | `max_tool_calls` | 5 | Maximum tool invocations per execution | Limits can be tightened per-tenant or per-request. They cannot be relaxed beyond the configured policy maximum. ### cgroup bounds (Linux) On Linux deployments, the engine applies cgroup constraints to the execution process: - **CPU quota**: limits CPU burst during local model inference - **Memory limit**: prevents unbounded memory growth in local inference - **I/O limits**: optional disk I/O rate limits for file-system tool use cgroup enforcement is independent of application code. An agent that attempts to consume more resources than its cgroup allows is throttled or killed by the kernel. --- ## Capability Enforcement Capabilities are enforced by the engine, not by the model. Even if the model generates output that attempts a disallowed tool call, the engine intercepts and rejects it before the call executes. The enforcement sequence: 1. Request arrives with a capability grant (or secure defaults are applied) 2. Engine validates the grant against the tenant's policy ceiling 3. Engine begins execution with the validated grant in scope 4. If the model attempts a tool call, the engine checks the grant before executing 5. If the call is outside the grant, the engine records a capability violation and rejects the call 6. Execution continues or terminates depending on the violation policy Violation events are recorded in the execution receipt. They cannot be suppressed. --- ## Secure Defaults The engine applies secure defaults when capability grants are not explicitly specified: | Setting | Default | |---|---| | `allow_http` | disabled | | `allow_shell` | disabled | | `allow_filesystem` | disabled | | `max_tokens` | 2048 | | `max_steps` | 5 | Tools must be explicitly enabled. The defaults assume no tool use is intended.

content: SDKs Support Matrix Support Policy Run A Registered Action JavaScript / TypeScript Other Languages Durable Tasks Native SDK Clients Go Rust Python Store a provider API key List registered fleet agents Experimental: Hosted Inference Clients Deployment Mode Guidance Code Quality Expectations # SDKs The production Igris integration path is **registered actions**: register an action once, then run it by name and inspect the durable run. That path is plain HTTP — `POST /v1/actions/:name/run` works from any language with any HTTP client — so an SDK is a convenience, not a requirement. - **Native Igris SDKs** add typed clients and helpers for actions (JavaScript/TypeScript), durable tasks, receipts, vault operations, runtimes, and behavior trees - **Plain HTTP** is the right answer for any language without a native SDK — every endpoint page in the [API reference](/docs/api-reference) includes ready-to-use cURL, JavaScript, Go, and Rust samples The native first-class SDKs are JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, and Python. Java, C#, and Ruby should call the Actions HTTP API directly today. For production integration guidance, reusable client construction, and environment-variable patterns, continue with [SDK Integration Patterns →](/docs/sdk-integration-patterns). ## Support Matrix ## Support Policy Treat the SDK table as a product support statement, not just a package list: - **First-class** means the language is part of the maintained customer SDK surface - **HTTP API** means the supported contract for that language today is the documented Actions HTTP API through any standard HTTP client If your team wants the strongest support commitment, choose JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, or Python. Every other language integrates cleanly over plain HTTP — the actions contract is small on purpose. --- ## Run A Registered Action ### JavaScript / TypeScript The JavaScript SDK wraps the actions gateway directly. `runAction` submits the run; with `wait: true` it polls until the run reaches a terminal state: typescript const client = new IgrisClient({ baseUrl: 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const run = await client.runAction( 'send_invoice', , , ); console.log(run.status, run.proof_status); The idempotency key is what makes retries safe: retrying with the same key inside your tenant returns the original run instead of running the action again. You can also fetch a run later by id: typescript const client = new IgrisClient({ baseUrl: 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const result = await client.getActionResult('018f4a2b-3c1e-7a2d-9b8f-4d5e6f7a8b9c'); console.log(result.status, re JavaScript / TypeScript first-class Preferred native SDK for browser and Node.js integrations. Python first-class Preferred native SDK for Python services, data pipelines, and scripting. Java http-api Call the Actions HTTP API directly until a native Java SDK is promoted explicitly. C# http-api Call the Actions HTTP API directly until a native C# SDK is promoted explicitly. Ruby http-api Call the Actions HTTP API directly until a native Ruby SDK is promoted explicitly.

title: SDK Integration Patterns
description: This guide shows how to use the SDK surface in a way that is maintainable in production.
content: SDK Integration Patterns Choose The Right Client Surface First Standard Environment Variables Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Pattern: Centralize Client Construction JavaScript / TypeScript Go Rust Pattern: Separate Hosted And Local Modes Cleanly JavaScript / TypeScript mode switch Pattern: Handle Product Errors Explicitly Pattern: Keep Receipt And Audit Handling Out Of The Hot Path Pattern: Start With One Action, Then Go Deeper Production Checklist Related Guides # SDK Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use the SDK surface in a way that is maintainable in production. It is not a language feature catalog. It is the set of patterns that keep integrations clean when the same product may be called in cloud, local-runtime, or hybrid deployments. --- ## Choose The Right Client Surface First Start with this decision: - The production integration path is the **Actions HTTP API**: register an action, run it by name with an idempotency key, inspect the run. It is one small contract and works from any language. - Use a native Igris SDK when you want a typed client on top of that — the JavaScript/TypeScript SDK wraps actions directly (`client.runAction`), and all native SDKs add helpers for durable tasks, receipts, vault operations, and runtimes. The first-class native SDKs today are: - JavaScript / TypeScript - Go - Rust - Python If you are in Java, C#, Ruby, or another language without a first-class native SDK, the safest default is the Actions HTTP API with your standard HTTP client. ## Standard Environment Variables Use the same environment-variable model across languages: - `IGRIS_API_KEY` for hosted API access - `IGRIS_BASE_URL` when you need to override the default base URL Recommended defaults: - hosted API: `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local runtime: `http://localhost:8080` Keeping this consistent is one of the easiest ways to make cloud, local, and hybrid deployments feel like one product to your own application teams. ## Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Do not let every handler decide whether it is in cloud, local, or hybrid mode. Make that a startup concern: - cloud mode points to `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local mode points to `http://localhost:8080` - hybrid mode usually still keeps application traffic on the hosted API, while Igris coordinates work with runtimes behind that surface The goal is to keep your business logic unaware of deployment details whenever possible. ## Pattern: Centralize Client Construction Do not scatter client creation across handlers and jobs. Create one small constructor per service and keep the auth/base-URL decision there. ### JavaScript / TypeScript typescript export function createIgrisClient() { const apiKey = process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY; if (!apiKey) { throw new Error('IGRIS_API_KEY is required'); } return new IgrisClient({ baseUrl: process.env.IGRIS_BASE_URL

title: Security
description: Igris security has two distinct planes:
content: Security Authentication Tenant API Keys Console Sessions Provider Keys Policy And Capability Controls Receipts And Verification Deployment Notes Compliance # Security Igris security has two distinct planes: - **Tenant API keys** for automation and programmatic access - **Console session cookies** for browser access to the web app Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Authentication ### Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys use the `igris_` prefix and are accepted in: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Best practices: - Store tenant API keys in environment variables - Rotate them if exposed - Scope usage to the tenant that owns the key bash export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_abc123..." ### Console Sessions The web console uses Better Auth session cookies. Those cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. Do not script console session access as generic bearer authorization headers. ### Provider Keys Provider keys stored through the current public vault API are encrypted before storage and returned only as masked values. --- ## Policy And Capability Controls A restrictive starting point in the current control-plane policy model looks like this: json { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_fs_write": false, "allow_external_api": false, "domain_allowlist": [], "domain_denylist": [], "writable_paths": [], "readable_paths": [], "violation_behavior": "terminate" } Start tight, then expand based on observed violations and actual agent requirements. --- ## Receipts And Verification Customer-facing verification routes currently live on the proof API: - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` - `GET /v1/proof/violations` Example: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' Treat that hosted verification route carefully. The stronger proof-backed cryptographic verification story is demonstrated in the local proof path; the hosted route should be described according to its current stored-value comparison and proof-status behavior. --- ## Deployment Notes - The local runtime can enforce its own API key with the local `auth` config - Fleet registration is gated by a valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` plus `IGRIS_API_KEY` - For local-only deployments, point clients directly at the runtime and keep your own storage if you need offline receipt retention --- ## Compliance Igris is positioned to support compliance workflows, but the exact operational mode
