title: Semantic Routing
description: Semantic routing is an advanced path-selection mechanism that classifies work before choosing among eligible execution paths.
content: Semantic Routing What It Does Where It Fits Decision Flow Fallback Behavior What To Expect Proof Language Related Pages # Semantic Routing Semantic routing is an advanced **Execute**-stage mechanism. Its job is to help Igris choose among eligible execution paths based on the kind of work being requested, instead of treating every request as identical. This is useful for advanced operators, but it is not the main reason to adopt Igris. Use [Request -> Execute -> Verify](/docs/request-execute-verify) for the primary product model. Use this page when you want the deeper path-selection detail. --- ## What It Does Semantic routing adds a classification step before final path selection. In practice, that means Igris can: - classify the request into a workload type - narrow the eligible providers or paths for that class - choose among those candidates with health and policy still applied This is meant to improve path selection for advanced workloads, not to override governance, policy, or verification. ## Where It Fits The simplified stack is: 1. policy decides what is allowed 2. health and trust narrow what is currently usable 3. semantic routing helps classify the work 4. final selection chooses the target path That layering matters because semantic routing should stay subordinate to safety and policy controls. ## Decision Flow text Request -> classification -> workload class -> eligible providers or paths -> final selection -> execution ## Fallback Behavior Semantic routing should not be a hard dependency for execution. If classification is unavailable, the system should still be able to continue with non-semantic path selection rather than turning classifier issues into execution outages. That is the operator-friendly reason to treat this as an advanced mechanism rather than a foundational identity claim. ## What To Expect Teams using semantic routing should expect: - class-specific path selection behavior - changing decisions as observations accumulate - the need for explicit policy overrides when deterministic routing is required Do not assume a semantic strategy stays fixed across time unless you pin the path explicitly. ## Proof Language Semantic routing is best treated as an advanced, source-confirmed capability. title: Shadow Mode
description: Shadow mode is an advanced comparison workflow that can run an observed parallel path without replacing the primary result.
content: Shadow Mode What It Does Why Teams Use It How To Read The Results Proof Language Cost And Scope Related Pages # Shadow Mode Shadow mode is an advanced comparison workflow. It can run an observed parallel path beside the primary execution path so operators can compare outcomes without immediately changing what the caller receives. That makes it useful for evaluation and tuning, but it should be treated as an advanced feature rather than a first-contact product claim. --- ## What It Does At a high level: text Request -> primary execution result returned -> shadow result captured separately for comparison The important idea is that the shadow path is for observation, not for replacing the primary path automatically. ## Why Teams Use It Shadow mode can help teams: - compare candidate providers or models - test a new configuration with lower risk - observe how an alternate path behaves before changing the primary path It is most useful when the team already has a stable baseline and wants to inspect alternatives carefully. ## How To Read The Results A shadow comparison is only useful if the team knows what it is looking for: - latency differences - cost differences - divergence in result shape or quality - differences in policy-sensitive behavior Treat the comparison output as decision support, not as a proof that the shadow path is ready for promotion. ## Proof Language Shadow mode is best treated as an advanced or preview-oriented capability unless you have deployment-specific evidence for the exact workflow you are describing. It is appropriate to explain the comparison model, but not to overstate its production-readiness across every environment. ## Cost And Scope Shadow execution may consume additional resources. Use it deliberately, with explicit scope and sampling decisions, rather than leaving it on broadly without a reason. ## Related Pages - [Speculative Execution →](/docs/speculative-execution) - [Execution Flow →](/docs/execution-flow) - [History & Alerts →](/docs/history) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status)

content: Service Level Agreement Availability Cloud API Scheduled Maintenance Performance API Response Times Support Response Times Support Scope Incident Management Incident Severity Levels Communication During Incidents Post-Incident Reports Data Retention Exclusions SLA Credits # Service Level Agreement This document describes service-level commitments for hosted Igris surfaces. Technical-preview and proof-limited areas are excluded unless explicitly stated. --- ## Availability ### Cloud API | Tier | Target Uptime | Monthly Downtime Budget | |---|---|---| | Seed | 99.5% | ~3.6 hours | | Horizon | 99.9% | ~43 minutes | | Infinite | 99.95% | ~22 minutes | Uptime is measured as the percentage of time the cloud API successfully processes requests, excluding scheduled maintenance windows. ### Scheduled Maintenance Scheduled maintenance windows are communicated at least 48 hours in advance via: - Email notification to the account owner - Banner notification in the console - Status page update at [status.igrisinertial.com](https://status.igrisinertial.com) Maintenance windows are limited to 4 hours per month and are scheduled during off-peak hours (02:00–06:00 UTC). --- ## Performance ### API Response Times The cloud API targets the following response time percentiles for inference routing decisions (excluding provider inference time): | Percentile | Target | |---|---| | P50 | < 50ms | | P95 | < 200ms | | P99 | < 500ms | Provider inference time depends on the selected provider and model and is not included in these targets. --- ## Support Response Times | Tier | Channel | Initial Response | Resolution Target | |---|---|---|---| | Seed | Email | Standard queue | Best effort | | Horizon | Priority email | Priority queue | 5 business days | | Infinite | Dedicated onboarding and security review support | Coordinated | Contracted with the engagement | ### Support Scope Support covers: - Platform functionality and configuration - API usage and integration guidance - Billing and subscription questions - Troubleshooting deployment issues - Bug reports and feature requests Support does not cover: - Custom development or integration work - Third-party provider issues (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) - Hardware troubleshooting for edge devices --- ## Incident Management ### Incident Severity Levels | Severity | Description | Example | |---|---|---| | **Critical** | Complete service outage affecting all tenants | Cloud API unreachable | | **High** | Major feature unavailable for a significant subset | Routing engine degraded | | **Medium** | Partial degradation or non-critical feature broken | Dashboard metrics delayed | | **Low** | Minor issue with workaro

title: SLO Enforcer
description: How Igris evaluates runtime and routing health against latency, error-rate, availability, and throughput objectives, and what is customer-facing today.
content: SLO Enforcer What Is Enforced Evaluation Output Customer-Facing Surfaces Operational Access Integration Guidance # SLO Enforcer Igris uses SLO enforcement to keep routing and runtime execution inside operational bounds. The enforcer evaluates live metrics, classifies breaches, and produces remediation actions that the platform can execute or record. The current customer-facing contract is not a standalone SLO configuration API. title: Speculative Execution
description: Speculative execution is an advanced path-selection mode that can race draft and primary execution paths for selected workloads.
content: Speculative Execution What It Does Where It Can Help What To Say Carefully Operational Reading Simulation And Analytics Related Features Proof Language Related Pages # Speculative Execution Speculative execution is an advanced execution mode. It can run a draft path in parallel with a primary path and decide whether the draft is good enough to return. This is useful for advanced latency-sensitive setups, but it should be treated as an optimization layer under the Execute stage, not as the core product story. --- ## What It Does At a high level: 1. a draft path starts 2. the primary path starts 3. the system decides whether the draft is acceptable 4. one result is returned The caller still receives one execution result. The internal race is an advanced mechanism, not a separate surface the application needs to learn first. ## Where It Can Help Speculative execution is most relevant when teams are experimenting with: - streaming workloads - predictable request types - advanced latency tuning It is less relevant for ordinary onboarding or for teams that have not yet established a stable baseline execution path. ## What To Say Carefully Do not assume speculative execution always improves latency or cost. The exact outcome depends on workload shape, provider behavior, and how often the draft path is accepted. This page intentionally does not promise headline percentage improvements without benchmark evidence for the environment in question. ## Operational Reading If you enable speculative execution, watch for: - acceptance rate - cost impact - path-selection stability - whether the workload is actually a good fit If acceptance is consistently low, the feature is probably adding complexity without enough benefit. ## Simulation And Analytics The product exposes speculative status, analytics, and simulation surfaces so operators can inspect how the mode behaves before using it broadly. Treat these surfaces as advanced evaluation tools, not as proof that the optimization is beneficial for every workload. ## Related Features - council and shadow features should be evaluated independently - receipts should still reflect the path that actually produced the returned result - proof claims should stay aligned with [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) ## Proof Language Speculative execution is best documented as an advanced, source-confirmed capability. Use production claims only when you have workload-specific evidence. ## Related Pages - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [Shadow Mode →](/docs/shadow-mode) - [Cloud Coordination →]

title: Swarm Coordination (Technical Preview)
description: Advanced coordination patterns for multiple execution environments and multi-path review workflows.
content: Swarm Coordination (Technical Preview) Two Advanced Patterns Multi-Path Review Environment Broadcast What To Expect Practical Guidance Related Pages # Swarm Coordination (Technical Preview) Swarm-oriented coordination in Igris is an advanced surface. It sits under the **Execute** stage and should not be treated as the default product path. If you are new to Igris, start with [Request -> Execute -> Verify](/docs/request-execute-verify) and [First Verified Run](/docs/first-verified-run). See [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before planning around this page. --- ## Two Advanced Patterns ### Multi-Path Review Some workflows send the same task through more than one model or provider path, then compare or synthesize outcomes. This can be useful for high-scrutiny tasks, but it increases cost and complexity and should be enabled deliberately. ### Environment Broadcast Other workflows coordinate actions across more than one execution environment. This is useful when operators need a consistent rollout, command, or state change across registered environments. --- ## What To Expect These patterns are best understood as: - advanced operator workflows - specialized coordination mechanisms - areas that require stronger proof before they should be marketed as broadly production-ready Do not assume autonomous fleet behavior, automatic failover, or guaranteed rollout semantics from the presence of these surfaces alone. --- ## Practical Guidance Use swarm-style features only when you need them for a specific operational reason: - coordinated rollout across registered environments - deliberate multi-path review for higher-confidence tasks - controlled experimentation on advanced execution behavior If your main need is governed execution with visibility and receipts, the default execution model is simpler and better proven. --- ## Related Pages - [Fleet Management →](/docs/fleet-management) - [Fleet Rollout Workflow →](/docs/fleet-rollout-workflow) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status)

title: Tamper-Evident Logs
description: Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can
content: Tamper-Evident Logs How It Works Chain Verification What's Recorded Export GET /v1/receipts/export Console Retention Audit Workflow # Tamper-Evident Logs Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can be altered, deleted, or inserted without detection. --- ## How It Works Each execution receipt contains: 1. **Envelope hash** — SHA-256 hash of the canonical execution envelope 2. **Previous hash** — SHA-256 hash of the previous receipt (forming a chain) 3. **Signature** — Ed25519 signature of the envelope using a device-bound key Each receipt links to the previous receipt via hash, forming a chain. Each receipt is signed with a device-bound key that exists only on the originating runtime. Tampering with any receipt invalidates its signature and breaks the chain — both of which are detected by the verification API. --- ## Chain Verification Receipts can be verified at any time to confirm chain integrity: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' Response: json { "valid": true, "signature_valid": true, "chain_intact": true, "previous_hash_matches": true } If any link in the chain is broken, verification fails and the specific broken link is identified. --- ## What's Recorded Every receipt records: | Category | Fields | |---|---| | **Identity** | Request ID, tenant ID, agent ID, device ID, timestamp | | **Inputs** | Prompt, system message, parameters | | **Outputs** | Model response, tool call results | | **Resources** | Tokens consumed, wall time, CPU/memory usage | | **Capabilities** | Grants applied, violations recorded | | **Policy** | Policy hash at time of execution | | **Routing** | Provider selected, fallback count, latency | | **Chain** | Envelope hash, previous hash, signature | --- ## Export Receipts can be exported for external audit workflows: ### GET /v1/receipts/export Export receipts in the selected format and time range. bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=json&range=7d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ --output receipts_export.json Supported formats: - `json` — raw JSON array of receipts - `csv` — flattened CSV for spreadsheet analysis - `ndjson` — newline-delimited JSON for streaming processing --- ## Console View and verify receipts at `/proof/receipts`: - Receipt listing wit

content: Tools Tool Overview HTTP Tool Shell Tool Filesystem Tool Tool Audit Trail # Tools Igris agents can call external tools: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. All tool use is governed by the execution envelope's capability grants and recorded in the execution receipt. --- ## Tool Overview | Tool | Capability required | Use | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | Call external APIs, webhooks, web services | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands in a sandboxed context | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, and list files | Tools are disabled by default. Each must be explicitly granted in the request's capability grant or in the tenant's policy. --- ## HTTP Tool The HTTP tool allows agents to make GET and POST requests to external endpoints. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true }, "tool_config": { "http": { "allowed_domains": ["api.example.com", "*.private.example.com"], "timeout_ms": 5000, "max_response_bytes": 65536 } } } **Security controls:** - **Domain allowlist**: agents can only reach configured domains. Wildcards are supported for subdomains. - **Timeout**: requests that exceed `timeout_ms` are aborted and the failure is recorded. - **Response size limit**: responses larger than `max_response_bytes` are truncated. If `allowed_domains` is empty, all domains are permitted. Leaving it empty is not recommended for production deployments. --- ## Shell Tool The shell tool allows agents to execute shell commands. Shell access is the most sensitive capability and should be granted only when necessary. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_shell": true }, "tool_config": { "shell": { "allowed_commands": ["ls", "cat", "grep", "python3"], "working_directory": "/workspace", "timeout_ms": 10000, "env_allowlist": ["PATH", "HOME"] } } } **Security controls:** - **Command allowlist**: only listed commands can be executed. Commands not on the list are rejected before execution. - **Working directory**: the shell is confined to the specified directory. Attempts to navigate outside it are blocked. - **Timeout**: commands that run longer than `timeout_ms` are killed. - **Environment**: only environment variables on the allowlist are passed to the child process. For each issue you will find the symptoms, the most likely cause, and the steps to fix it. --- ## Runtime Not Starting ### Port already in use **Symptoms:** The runtime process exits immediately with an address binding error. Nothing appears in **Fleet → Devices**. **Cause:** Another process is already listening on the port the runtime is configured to use (default: 8080). **Fix:** Identify the conflicting process and stop it, or configure the runtime to use a different port. On Linux and macOS you can check what is using a port with: bash lsof -i :8080 After freeing the port or reconfiguring, restart the runtime. --- ### Missing API key **Symptoms:** The runtime starts but exits with an authentication error. No registration appears in the console. **Cause:** The runtime was started without a valid Igris API key in its configuration. **Fix:** Add your API key to the runtime's config file or pass it as the appropriate environment variable for your deployment method. Your API key is available in **Settings → Keys** in the console. If you do not see an API key, generate one from **Settings → Billing → Manage Account**. --- ### Config file not found **Symptoms:** The runtime exits with a message indicating it cannot find or parse the configuration file. **Cause:** The runtime is looking for its configuration file at the default path and it either does not exist or has a syntax error. **Fix:** Verify that the config file is present at the expected path. Check the file for YAML/TOML syntax errors — most runtimes print the line number of the first error. If you are using a custom path, confirm you are passing the correct path argument when starting the runtime. --- ## Runtime Not Appearing In The Console Environment View ### Network or firewall blocking outbound registration **Symptoms:** The runtime starts and appears to be running (the local health endpoint responds) but never appears in the console environment view. **Cause:** Outbound HTTPS traffic to `overture.igrisinertial.com` is being blocked by a firewall rule, proxy, or network policy. **Fix:** Verify connectivity from the runtime host: bash curl -v https://overture.igrisinertial.com/health If this fails, work with your network administrator to allow outbound HTTPS (port 443) to `overture.igrisinertial.com`. description: This guide covers how to upgrade between Igris versions, migrate data, and handle breaking changes.
content: Upgrade & Migration Versioning Upgrading the Runtime Manual Upgrade Is The Default Recommended Path Compare with the checksum shown in the console Or if running directly: pkill igris-runtime && igris-runtime serve Coordinated Rollout Surfaces Configuration Migration Config File Format Changes Backing Up Configuration Migrating Config Fields Data Migration Execution Receipts Execution Environment Configuration Provider Keys Behavior Tree Definitions Breaking Changes by Version Runtime v1.8.0 (March 2026) Runtime v1.7.x (March 2026) Runtime v1.6.0 (February 2026) Runtime v0.4.0 (November 2025) Rollback Checking for Updates Via Console Via API Via CLI Support # Upgrade & Migration This guide covers how to upgrade between Igris versions, migrate data, and handle breaking changes. --- ## Versioning Igris uses semantic versioning for the runtime binary: - **Major version** (v1 → v2): Breaking changes. Requires migration steps. - **Minor version** (v1.6 → v1.7): New features, backward compatible. - **Patch version** (v1.6.0 → v1.6.1): Bug fixes, backward compatible. The cloud API is versioned independently and maintains backward compatibility within a major version. --- ## Upgrading the Runtime ### Manual Upgrade Is The Default Recommended Path For Seed tier or manual deployments: 1. Download the new binary: bash curl -fsSL https://igrisinertial.com/install | bash Or download from **Fleet → Downloads** in the console. 2. Verify the checksum: bash sha256sum /usr/local/bin/igris-runtime # Compare with the checksum shown in the console 3. Restart the runtime: bash sudo systemctl restart igris-runtime # Or if running directly: # pkill igris-runtime && igris-runtime serve 4. Verify the upgrade: bash igris-runtime --version curl http://localhost:8080/health ### Coordinated Rollout Surfaces Some deployments may expose coordinated rollout or console-assisted update workflows for registered execution environments. Treat those as environment-management surfaces whose stronger OTA or automated rollout claims depend on proof status and deployment reality. If you need the most conservative upgrade story, use the manual path above and expand gradually with your own validation gates. --- ## Configuration Migration ### Config File Format Changes When upgrading between major versions, the configuration file format may change. The runtime will log warnings for deprecated fields and use defaults for new required fields. **Before upgrading, review the changelog for configuration changes.** ### Backing Up Configuration Always back up your configuration before upgrading: bash cp ~/.config/igris/config.json5 ~/.config/igris/config.json5.bak ### Migrating Config Fields If the upgrade includes config format changes, the runtime will: 1. Log a warning for each deprecated field 2. Use the default value for new required fields 3. title: Verification
description: How to inspect execution metadata, signed records, receipt hashes, and current proof-route behavior in Igris.
content: Verification Verification Inputs Proven Local Verification Path Cloud Proof Route Semantics What To Check After A Run Choosing The Right Verification Surface Verification Language To Use Carefully # Verification Verification is the part of Igris that answers: what happened, what record came back, and what can actually be checked? The short version is: - some verification behavior is proven locally today - some proof-oriented routes are useful record-comparison surfaces - not every verification surface is equally strong --- ## Verification Inputs Depending on the route, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata such as route decisions and provider labels - a signed `execution_envelope` - a signed `execution_receipt` - receipt hashes - receipt-log entries and previous-hash linkage These are not interchangeable. Execution history is not the same thing as a signed receipt, and a proof-status lookup is not the same thing as cryptographic verification. ## Proven Local Verification Path The strongest demonstrated verification path today is the local unified proof: bash ./scripts/unified_execution_proof_demo.sh That flow verifies: - the returned execution envelope signature - the returned execution receipt signature - the returned execution receipt hash - receipt presence in the local receipt log - receipt-chain linkage This is the current **proven locally** path. ## Cloud Proof Route Semantics The hosted proof route is: text POST /proof/receipts/verify Its current handler compares submitted values against the stored receipt record and returns the current verification state. It is useful when you want to check whether a stored receipt matches a supplied hash or signature value. Important caveat: - The current handler does **not** perform full cryptographic signature verification by itself. - It compares stored versus submitted values and returns fields such as `verified`, `verification_status`, `hash_valid`, and `signature_matches`. That means you should not describe this route as a full public cryptographic verifier in first-contact docs. ## What To Check After A Run When a run matters, inspect at least these layers: 1. **Execution metadata** for route decision and provider context 2. **Signed records** for the returned envelope or receipt material 3. **Proof status** for what the current route can confirm 4. **Receipt export or storage path** if another system will depend on the record later ## Choosing The Right Verification Surface | Need | Best current path | |---|---| | Prove the repo's local execution flow end to end | [First Verified Run](/doc
